articles.title: Russia kills at least 12 on sixth night of drone attacks on Kyiv
articles.body:
At least 12 people have been killed in and around Kyiv overnight as Ukraine’s capital endured a sixth consecutive night of Russian drone and missile attacks aimed at shattering infrastructure and lowering the morale of the city.
Eight of the dead were reported killed in Kyiv, including seven at a railway depot on the city’s left bank, and four were killed in Boryspil, to the east of the city, in a wave of strikes at about 2.30am after hours of air alerts.
A further four people were killed in other parts of Ukraine, regional officials said, in 28 waves of attacks that included a strike on a border crossing point with Romania on the Danube at Orlivka.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, said “a significant number of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles were used in the attack” and that Russia was taking advantage of a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors.
In a morning post on social media, Zelenskyy said: “Russia always plans its strikes specifically to cause as much destruction to people’s lives as possible, and it succeeds only when air defence capabilities are insufficient.”
Kyiv and the surrounding towns and villages have come under sustained attack in the past few days. Thirty-eight people were killed after a Russian drone struck an ammunition store in Myla, 15 miles west of Kyiv, on Thursday, the hit causing hours of secondary explosions and damaging nearby homes.
Ukraine’s air force said Russia had attacked 28 locations, focusing on the cities of Kyiv and Odesa and their surroundings. Air defences shot down five Iskander ballistic missiles, two Banderol and five Kalibr cruise missiles and 187 out of 218 drones. Officials no longer reveal the total numbers of missiles fired.
Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, the chief executive of Ukrainian Railways, said six of the seven people killed in and around the depot were employees of the network. Another rail worker was hospitalised, he added.
Kyiv has been chronically short of air defence systems since the supply of Patriot interceptors dried up. The Patriots are the only weapon that can effectively stop high-speed Russian ballistic missiles, made at the rate of about 60 a month.
Lockheed Martin, the US company that makes the most capable Pac-3 interceptors, produces about 600 a year, but US military supplies have been depleted during the US war with Iran. Ukraine is trying to secure a stockpile of about 300 for the winter, paid for by European allies, in a supply deal agreed with the US.
Moscow appears to be trying to take advantage of an absence of air defence capability before winter, in an escalation of a conflict nearly deadlocked on the frontline. Ukraine has been responding by attacking oil refineries, warehouses and other military facilities deep inside Russia, aiming to hurt the country’s economy.
Ukraine’s GUR military intelligence said it had attacked an oil refinery at the Baltic port of Ust-Luga, about 550 miles (885km) from its border. Russian officials said a civilian was killed in the border Belgorod region in an attack.
Russia captured 35 square miles (56 sq km) of Ukraine’s territory during August, analysis by the AFP news agency concluded. It was Moscow’s largest advance since February but still much lower than the 150 square mile a month average of 2025.
There remains little serious diplomatic effort to end the war, although on Monday India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, urged Vladimir Putin to end the war in public remarks at a bilateral meeting in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.
“Every day that the war continues, humanity is, in effect, set back a step, while every step towards peace gives all of humanity real hope for peace. We need to move from endless war to an end to the war,” Modi said.
Putin appeared impatient, tapping his feet as he listened. “Thank you very much, prime minister. We are moving forward along this path,” he replied.

articles.title: After a month-long lull in violence, Trump vows to hit iran hard
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has pledged to respond to Iranian strikes on US military personnel in Jordan and UAE, vowing "we're going to hit them hard". Trump also claimed the strait is in "extremely good shape" and Iran's financial system, military, and leadership have been largely degraded
Iran will "immediately" reciprocate if the US fulfils its commitments under an interim deal signed in June to end the six-month war and open the Strait of Hormuz, the Iranian president announced
Israeli attacks continue on Gaza, occupied West Bank, south Lebanon, and southern Syria despite any agreements or apparent ceasefires
And so we continue our live coverage of the day...
The Freedom Flotilla Coalition (FFC) has announced a new international mission challenging Israel’s blockade of Gaza, with vessels travelling between European ports before a planned attempt to reach Gaza in October.
FFC vessel Handala II sailed around Scandinavia in June and July, stopping in Norway, Sweden and Denmark.
Earlier this month, the vessel Kate departed Bristol and has since made port calls in Ireland, Germany and France. It is due to continue to Spain, Portugal and Italy before sailing towards Gaza.
At each stop, the coalition said it will hold public events and campaign for governments to end what it describes as complicity in Israel’s actions in Gaza.
“The Freedom Flotilla sails again because our governments continue to fail to uphold their obligations,” said Zohar Chamberlain Regev, an FFC Steering Committee member. “At every port, we will carry the demand that Palestinians be free to live with dignity. In October, we intend to carry that demand and the solidarity of people around the world to Gaza’s shores.”
The announcement comes months after Israel intercepted a previous flotilla mission and detained more than 430 activists from around the world.
Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir also faced widespread condemnation after posting footage appearing to mock and threaten detained activists.
Iran parliament speaker urges citizens to cut petrol use
A top Iranian official called on citizens to curb their petrol consumption on Tuesday, as the country faces difficulty importing enough fuel to meet demand due to a US naval blockade.
"Of course, part of the responsibility for this high consumption does not lie with our people; it lies with our industry," parliament speaker and top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said in a televised address. "But in any case, what is clear is that we need to save gasoline in our consumption."
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian on Tuesday vowed to match any US move to return to a June deal aimed at ending their war and thanked Russia's Vladimir Putin for Moscow's stance on the conflict during an international summit.
Russia and Iran -- two of the most sanctioned countries in the world -- have massively deepened their military and trade ties during Moscow's invasion of Ukraine.
Putin and Pezeshkian held talks on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, bringing together more than a dozen leaders -- including Putin, China's Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
They met a day after US President Donald Trump -- who has warned Moscow and Beijing against arming Tehran -- threatened to hit Iran "hard" after the foes traded fire for the first time in weeks.
Pezeshkian told the summit that if the United States returns to the deal aimed at ending months of hostilities, Iran "will immediately take reciprocal action", according to the Iranian presidency's website.
The deal, meant to set the stage for final peace talks, has collapsed as both sides accused each other of violating its terms.
Pezeshkian also warned Tuesday that a return by the United States to "a policy of pressure and threats" risked derailing diplomatic efforts to end the war.
He later met Putin, telling him: "We appreciate and thank you for your positions at every stage".
US likely to announce Iran bank sanctions this week: Bessent
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday the United States is likely to announce sanctions on a bank this week as part of its economic campaign against Iran.
"We are probably going to announce a bank sanction this week, and we will announce one the week after. We are speaking to our allies here, who have all come forward, and we have had a great show of support," Bessent said.
The approaching rainy season risks worsening a dire public health crisis in Gaza, where most people live in overcrowded tent camps amid rubble and overflowing sewage, the WHO warned Tuesday.
The World Health Organisation warned that there had already been a clear deterioration in the quality of water reaching the population in recent months, while the number of diarrhoea cases had surged.
"Whilst we fail to provide people with the minimum quantities of water, water quality and water contamination remains a major issue," said Reinhilde Van de Weerdt, the WHO's representative in the Palestinian territories.
Gaza has been engulfed in a devastating health and humanitarian crisis since Israel launched its war in the territory on October 2023.
Despite a US-backed ceasefire that took effect in October 2025, Israeli attacks have not halted in the Gaza Strip, and it continues to impose significant restrictions on the entry of goods, including medical equipment and fuel.
In April, Doctors Without Borders said that Israel was using water access as a "weapon" in Gaza, pointing to data from the United Nations, European Union and World Bank indicating that Israel had destroyed or damaged nearly 90 percent of water and sanitation infrastructure in the territory.
In April, MSF said that Israel was using water access as a "weapon" in Gaza. [Getty]
Iran president thanks Putin for Russia's stance during war
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian held talks on Tuesday with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan, the Iranian presidency said.
"During the meeting, the latest state of bilateral relations between Iran and Russia was reviewed and the two sides discussed ways to strengthen and expand cooperation in various fields," said the presidency in a statement accompanied by images of Putin and Pezeshkian shaking hands.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin for Moscow's stance during the US-Israeli war on Iran, in their first meeting since the conflict broke out on 28 Februrary.
"We appreciate and thank you for your positions at every stage, both during the period when the fighting and acts of aggression were taking place and under normal circumstances, when the United States was imposing sanctions on us, both at the United Nations and in international forums," Pezeshkian told Putin at a meeting.
Shanghai Cooperation Org condemns US-Israel war on Iran
The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation expressed "deep concern over developments in the Middle East and around Iran".
Member nations at the summits inauguration affirmed their "position condemning military strikes on the territory of the Islamic Republic of Iran, which have resulted in numerous civilian casualties and significant damage to the country's economy".
"Such actions violate the principles and norms of international law and the UN Charter and create serious risks to international peace, security and stability," it said.
Qatar urges US, Iran to resume talks after flare-up
Mediator Qatar on Tuesday urged the United States and Iran to return to negotiations after they renewed tit-for-tat attacks.
On Sunday, the US carried out strikes on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran quickly retaliating by attacking US military targets in the Middle East.
After six months of war, the foes remain at an impasse, with Iran disrupting traffic in the strategic Strait of Hormuz with its blockade and the US persisting with a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
"We have said from day one that leaving the issue unresolved and trying to normalise the closure of the Strait would lead to escalation," Qatari foreign ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari told a regular press briefing.
"This is precisely what we have witnessed over the past two days," he said.
"We urge the parties to exercise wisdom and return to the negotiating path, and we continue to intensify our efforts with our mediation partners to ensure a return to that path."
Earlier on Tuesday, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran would "immediately" reciprocate if the United States returned to a June deal aimed at ending their war.
"In Qatar, in the region, in the world today, we cannot afford to accept the status quo," Al Ansari said.
"Discussions with our mediation partners—whether in Pakistan or Oman—are ongoing," he added.
Last week, Qatar's Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani travelled to Tehran as part of the mediation efforts, after Iran and Oman, which border the key strait, said they were discussing a temporary shipping corridor and the clearance of mines.
Gaza's roadmap to nowhere: Why Israel won't give up control
For Netanyahu and Israel's opposition, the Gaza status quo offers territorial control and military freedom without the burden of reconstruction, writes Muhammad Shehada.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said Tuesday that his country was working towards a "diplomatic solution" with Israel, with US mediation, despite ongoing Israeli attacks.
Israel has launched hundreds of strikes on Syria since longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad was overthrown in December 2024.
"The attacks are still ongoing. We observed 65 incursions in July alone, and 52 in the first 18 days of August," Shaibani told a press conference with his visiting Danish counterpart Lars Lokke Rasmussen.
He slammed a "campaign of raids on homes in Quneitra province and the Damascus countryside", and said Syria had registered 147 cases of Israeli troops detaining Syrians so far this year, with "49 of them still detained".
"Despite these challenges, we are still committed to the option of a diplomatic solution and we are working seriously to achieve this," Shaibani said, adding: "We are engaged in negotiations mediated by the United States of America."
A "senior figure" was abducted in Gaza, announced by Defense Minister Israel Katz, who claimed that the individual is "the head of Hamas' General Security, who managed the organization's counterintelligence and intelligence operations."
Iran president says US threats risk derailing diplomacy
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tuesday that a return by the United States to a policy of pressure and threats risked derailing diplomatic efforts to end the war in the Middle East.
"The repeated violation by the United States of its commitments under the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding showed that... the absence of effective enforcement guarantees and a return to a policy of pressure and threats could derail the path of diplomacy," Pezeshkian said in a speech at a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan.
Pezeshkian spoke at a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan. [Getty]
Funding cuts force UN's WFP to halve West Bank aid
The United Nations' food agency warned Tuesday that funding cuts were forcing it to slash the number of aid recipients in the occupied West Bank in half, warning of dire consequences.
The World Food Programme said that from this month it would be reducing the number of people it reaches with food aid in the Palestinian territory from 400,000 to 200,000.
"WFP is being forced to reduce the number of people we assist in the West Bank by half," Shaun Hughes, the agency's representative in the Palestinian territories, told reporters in Geneva.
"This is happening as the food needs in the West Bank are more than double what they were two years ago," he warned, speaking from London.
He pointed out that food insecurity had not traditionally been a major problem in the West Bank.
But he argued that since the Gaza war began in October 2023, "intensified settler violence, prolonged and escalating Israeli military operations, severe movement restrictions, demolitions and widespread displacement in the West Bank have eroded Palestinian livelihoods and contributed to increased food insecurity."
The WFP said that its latest quarterly food security analysis found that 76 percent of households in the occupied West Bank had experienced a significant decline in income, with many families forced to sell assets and reduce the number and quality of their meals to survive.
The analysis found that a third of families could not afford a nutritious diet due to the rapidly deteriorating economy, the agency said, adding that those living in rural areas and in the southern West Bank governorates were the most affected.
"Families who were once thriving and earning a living from their land are now unable to afford enough food," Hughes said.
Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967.
Israeli attacks in Gaza kills four, including three children
Israeli gunfire and airstrikes killed at least four people, including three children, in the Gaza Strip on Tuesday, health officials said.
Witnesses said Israeli warplanes fired at least 12 missiles near the Katiba area in the west of Gaza City, an area crowded with displaced families.
At least three people—two children and a woman—were killed and several others wounded in the unusually heavy bombardment, medics said. Two vehicles were hit and reduced to twisted wreckage.
In a statement on Tuesday, the Israeli military said it struck several targets in the Gaza Strip in order to remove threats to Israeli security forces.
Ismail Al-Thawabta, director of the Hamas-run Gaza government media office, said an Israeli special force had attempted to carry out an operation in Gaza City but was discovered during the mission.
He said Israel then launched heavy airstrikes involving more than 10 warplanes, killing and wounding several people.
In a separate incident, medics said a girl, Israa Al-Hissi, was killed and two other people were wounded when Israeli forces operating east of Deir Al-Balah in central Gaza opened fire on the area.
Israeli settlers set mosque on fire near Nablus, West Bank
At dawn this morning, Israeli settlers set fire a mosque in the village of Bazaria, northwest of Nablus in the occupied West Bank, reported Palestinian media.
The Palestinian Ministry of Endowments and Religious Affairs condemned the attack, and considered it a dangerous escalation targeting mosques and places of worship. The ministry noted that these attacks have been ongoing with no accountability.
Mosques in the occupied West Bank and Jerusalem are subjected to repeated attacks by the Israeli army and settlers. So far, 11 mosques have faced arson attacks since the beginning of 2026, in addition to vandalising their contents, destroying the Qur’an, preventing the call to prayer and performing prayers and other abuses.
EU's Kallas: Hormuz diplomatic efforts produced 'no results'
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said diplomatic efforts over opening the Hormuz are continuing but have not produce a breakthrough.
"The freedom of navigation needs to be respected. The diplomatic efforts are still ongoing, but no results at the moment. For us, it is important that there are no tolls, no fees for these routes that have been open before," Kallas said in Ireland ahead of a ministers meeting.
Kallas said the meeting will also examine a possible European mission to support the Lebanese military in south Lebanon.
Three "unknown projectiles" struck a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz overnight, a British maritime agency said Tuesday following a fresh flare-up in the US-Israeli war on Iran thats pasted six months.
Tehran has imposed an effective blockade of the strait since the United States and Israel launched their war in late February.
It says it wants to charge fees for passage and has attacked ships it accuses of attempting to circumvent its preferred route through the waterway.
In response, the United States has imposed a rival blockade of Iranian ports.
"A tanker has reported being struck by 3 unknown projectiles whilst completing an outbound transit of the Strait of Hormuz," the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said on X early Tuesday.
The incident occurred 17 nautical miles (31 kilometres) east of the Oman city of Khasab, it added.
No casualties or environmental impact were reported, the agency said.
Maritime security company Vanguard Tech later identified the ship as the Liberia-flagged Senegal Prosperity.
"The rockets impacted the vessel's port side, engine room and ballast tank, resulting in a loss of communications," Vanguard said, adding that the crew were safe.
Attacks on commercial ships in the strait, which was free to transit before the war, previously led to the collapse of an April ceasefire between the United States and Iran.
Ongoing trauma, uncertainty for Gaza's missing children
For Samar Doghmosh, a Palestinian woman from war-torn Gaza, every day begins with the same question: Is her 11-year-old son Mu'taz alive or dead?
In December 2024, Mu'taz left his family's tent in eastern Deir al-Balah, in central Gaza, to fetch water. He never returned. Nearly two years later, his mother is still searching for an answer.
"Some people tell us he was killed and that stray dogs devoured his body. Others say he was injured. The last person who saw him said he was arrested by the Israeli army," Doghmosh told The New Arab.
The family contacted the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) after Mu'taz disappeared, hoping the organisation could determine whether he had been detained or locate information about his whereabouts.
Oil prices climbed further and Asian shares were mixed Tuesday as recurring violence in the Iran war after more than a month with no significant fighting heightened uncertainty over the future of the conflict.
Shares in online fast-fashion retailer Shein fell as much as 10% after they began trading in Hong Kong on Tuesday. By midday they were 5% lower.
Brent crude gained 0.8% to $91.23 per barrel. It gained 2.7% on Monday after the US attacked rocket launchers on an Iranian island on Sunday, saying they were preparing to launch mines into the Strait of Hormuz. Iran responded by launching missiles at US sites in Jordan, all of which were intercepted.
The war has curtailed traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, which once accounted for about 20% of the world’s oil shipments. Oil prices remain high after an initial surge earlier in the war, and that has made everything from gasoline to shipped goods more expensive.
US benchmark crude was up 1% at $86.62 per barrel.
Turkey says regional defence pact not a response to any one
Turkey's top diplomat stressed Monday the regional defence pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia was not aimed at any particular country and open to others, including Egypt.
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan's remarks came after the first ministerial meeting of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement which commits Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia to mutual defence in the event of any of them being attacked.
Preliminary data tracking maritime traffic, issued today, Tuesday, showed that the number of ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz yesterday, Monday, were at only five ships, with no significant change compared to Saturday and Sunday.
This number is much lower than the average recorded over ten days, which amounts to about 14 ships.
According to data from the “Kepler” platform, four of those ships entered the strait while one ship left it.
Iran president: reciprocate if US returns to June deal
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tuesday that Tehran would "immediately" reciprocate if the United States returned to a June deal aimed at ending their war.
"I state explicitly that if the United States returns to its commitments under the aforementioned memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately take reciprocal action," Pezeshkian said at a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan, according to the website of the Iranian presidency.

articles.title: Drone attack damages Russia’s Baltic oil port as drone crosses Latvia into Estonia
articles.body:
Russian authorities reported damage and a fire at Ust-Luga port during an overnight drone attack on 1 September. One drone crossed Latvian and Estonian airspace, prompting NATO to scramble Turkish F-16s.
The attack hit a major outlet for Russian energy exports. Reuters reported that Ust-Luga loads about 700,000 barrels of crude a day and exported 32.9 million metric tons of oil products in 2025. Its terminals also serve shadow-fleet tankers used to bypass sanctions.
Leningrad Oblast Governor Alexander Drozdenko said emergency crews were working in Ust-Luga’s port zone while the damage was being assessed. He later claimed Russian air defenses downed 52 drones over Leningrad Oblast and reported no casualties.
Drozdenko did not identify the damaged facility or specify the scale of the fire.
Militarnyi published an image attributed to the Exilenova+ monitoring channel showing a blaze near the port. The image’s time and precise location have not been independently verified.
There was no immediate information on whether the attack disrupted port operations. Ukraine had not claimed responsibility at the time of publication.
The regional warnings coincided with a broader drone attack on western Russia that included Ust-Luga, although authorities did not specifically link the drones approaching or entering NATO airspace to the port strike.
Baltic states issue warnings as NATO fighters scramble, while Finland restricts traffic
Estonia warned residents in eight counties and scrambled Turkish fighter jets serving in NATO’s Baltic Air Defense Mission, which protects the skies of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania.
Estonian Air Force Commander Brigadier General Riivo Valge said around a dozen drones had moved near the country’s border. One briefly entered southeastern Estonia, while another approached Narva before turning back into Russia. The fighters did not open fire, and the warnings were lifted by about 5:30 a.m.
Latvia issued two warnings overnight, first in the Ludza municipality and then in the Alūksne municipality. Latvia’s Armed Forces said a drone crossed Latvian airspace and continued into Estonia, where NATO fighters searched for it. The Latvian alerts ended at around 4:20 a.m.
Finland’s Armed Forces introduced temporary air and sea restrictions over the eastern Gulf of Finland at 3:37 a.m.
The military lifted both restrictions shortly after 6 a.m., saying no drones had strayed into Finland.
Repeated strikes on Ust-Luga
Ust-Luga lies around 110 kilometers west of St. Petersburg and some 900 kilometers from Ukraine. It is the endpoint of the Baltic Pipeline System-II, which carries Russian crude to the port for export. The area hosts facilities operated by Russian gas producer NOVATEK and fertilizer maker EuroChem.
Ukraine began its series of 2026 attacks on Ust-Luga overnight on 24–25 March. The Security Service of Ukraine, the country’s counterintelligence agency, and the military’s elite Special Operations Forces confirmed that they had struck NOVATEK’s gas-condensate complex, which processes liquid hydrocarbons into fuels.
Further attacks followed in late March. They set fuel-storage tanks ablaze, damaged a pier and pumping equipment, and temporarily halted port operations, according to Russian Telegram channel Astra.
On 7 April, Ukraine’s General Staff, the military’s senior command, confirmed another strike on Ust-Luga’s oil terminal, saying three oil storage tanks were destroyed. Another attack on 14 August again caused damage and a fire, Drozdenko reported at the time.

articles.title: Farhad Ibragimov: Türkiye is one missile deal away from crossing Russia’s red line
articles.body:
Farhad Ibragimov: Türkiye is one missile deal away from crossing Russia’s red line
Recently, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said that Moscow was still waiting for clarification from the US and Türkiye regarding possible arms supplies to Ukraine. Russia expects a response, as this matter directly affects not only bilateral relations but also the prospects for resolving the Ukraine crisis.
The issue goes far beyond the scope of yet another military-technical deal. In July, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan called for preventing the spread of the Russia-Ukraine conflict to the Black Sea region and advocated for the continuation of Ankara-mediated negotiations between Moscow and Kiev within the framework of the so-called Istanbul format. Türkiye emphasized that the security of shipping and energy infrastructure is of fundamental importance to it.
The Russian side, in turn, points out an obvious contradiction. According to Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, Ankara and Washington, in their contacts with Moscow, stated that they sent Kiev signals about the unacceptability of attacks in the Black Sea. However, Moscow has not received a public or equally strong response from Türkiye and the US concerning Ukrainian drone strikes on commercial vessels and the infrastructure of the Caspian Pipeline Consortium near Novorossiysk. The Russian Foreign Ministry also warned that strikes on infrastructure and vessels used for delivering Western weapons to Ukraine would continue until the security threats in the region of the Azov and Black seas are eliminated.
Leaving diplomatic language aside, the question is very simple: can Türkiye simultaneously supply Kiev with weapons capable of being used against Russian targets and demand that Moscow continue to consider it a neutral intermediary?
What do the American documents actually state?
The US Congressional Record, published on August 6, shows two notifications about the proposed permanent transfer of American weapons from Turkish stockpiles to Ukraine. The first package includes 12 M270 MLRS launchers, 2,524 M26 unguided rockets with cluster munitions, and 47,000 M509A1 203mm cluster artillery shells. Their initial procurement price is listed at $255.9 million.
The second notification concerns 70 M39 ATACMS tactical ballistic missiles with an initial procurement price of approximately $28 million. In total this amounts to approximately $283.9 million. However, it would be incorrect to automatically assume that this is the price of the current contract since the terms of the potential deal between Ankara and Kiev have not been publicly disclosed.
Another point is equally important. The documents do not prove that the weapons have already been transferred to Kiev. They only confirm that the Turkish government proposed re-export, and the US Department of State notified Congress of its readiness to approve it after the statutory review period. Ankara cites the desire to get rid of outdated weapons and redirect funds toward modernizing its armed forces as the reason for the re-export. Kiev, according to the documents, intends to use these systems to enhance its offensive and defensive firepower.
This formulation makes the situation particularly serious. This isn’t about armored vehicles, communications equipment, or individual commercial drones; M39 ATACMS missiles are capable of engaging targets at ranges of up to 165 km and carry cluster munitions. Combined with M270 launchers and thousands of rocket and artillery munitions, this constitutes a comprehensive package of enhanced long-range firepower systems. Its possible use will inevitably entail losses among Russian troops and the risk of strikes deep into Russian territory.
Between mediation and participation
Russian-Turkish relations have never been an alliance in the strict sense of the word. Moscow and Ankara supported opposing sides in Syria and Libya; they hold different views on the status of Crimea, and compete for influence in various corners of Eurasia. Türkiye supplied Ukraine with drones, developed military-technical cooperation with it and consistently supported it. Yet, none of this prevented Russia and Türkiye from building gas pipelines, a nuclear power plant, developing trade, and reaching agreements in areas where their interests coincided.
This format was based on an unspoken rule that competition should not escalate into direct, critical damage to the other side. Strong disagreements could arise, but they remained manageable and were offset by cooperation in other areas.
The proposed transfer of ATACMS missiles, M270 launchers, and tens of thousands of cluster munitions brings Ankara dangerously close to the limits of this model of interaction. This is not a matter of one weapons system, but its purpose, the scale of the package, and the political context.
Türkiye isn’t simply offering to sell Kiev a batch of its own military equipment; it intends to transfer a large stockpile of American weapons intended to enhance Kiev’s firepower in the ongoing conflict with Russia, and is doing so with Washington’s approval.
Against this backdrop, Türkiye’s peacemaking rhetoric is starting to look increasingly unconvincing. Clearly, a mediator doesn’t have to be completely equidistant from the parties, but both sides should be able to trust it, at least on a minimum level. A mediator can’t call for a moratorium on strikes in the Black Sea while simultaneously helping one of the sides expand its weapons stockpiles; it can’t propose Istanbul as a platform for negotiations while strengthening Kiev’s military potential under the pretext of getting rid of outdated weapons.
Ankara risks overestimating Moscow’s patience
A familiar argument is being voiced by Turkish experts: Russian-Turkish relations are so deep and multifaceted, they argue, that a single deal can’t destroy them. There’s certainly some truth to that. Neither Russia nor Türkiye want to replay the scenario of the 2015 crisis. Severing ties would be detrimental to both sides.
However, Ankara is drawing an all-too-convenient conclusion that economic interdependence guarantees impunity for any foreign policy maneuver; and this is a dangerous fallacy. The Turkish leadership apparently confuses freedom of maneuver with the absence of a price to be paid for that maneuver.
Russia indeed benefits from the Turkish market, transit routes, and bilateral trade, and this is apparent to all. Türkiye remains an important economic and regional partner for Moscow. However, the dependence of the parties is not symmetrical across all sectors. In recent years, the Russian economy has demonstrated its ability to redirect raw material flows, restructure logistics, and seek new markets. Russia’s size allows it to do this quite well. For Türkiye, however, a sudden reduction in Russian energy supplies, tourism, investment, or access to the Russian market creates a more immediate and concentrated effect.
In 2025, trade between the two countries exceeded $50 billion. Russia retained a significant advantage in the trade structure: Türkiye primarily imports Russian energy resources and raw materials. That same year, it received approximately 22 billion cubic meters of gas from Russia; despite diversification, the share of Russian gas in Türkiye’s supply remained around 37%. Nearly seven million Russians visited Türkiye in 2025, securing Russia as the top source market for Türkiye’s tourism industry.
Finally, Russia is financing and constructing the Akkuyu Nuclear Power Plant at a cost of over $20 billion. Once operational, it is expected to supply up to 10% of Türkiye’s total electricity demand. At the end of 2025, Ankara announced an additional $9 billion in Russian financing for the project, part of which is expected to arrive in 2026–2027.
For an economy with an annual inflation rate of nearly 32% (as of July 2026), high borrowing costs, and chronic sensitivity to the price of imported energy, the loss of even a portion of these advantages will not be trivial. It will hit foreign exchange earnings, production costs, the balance of payments, and employment in tourism. The Turkish economy may not collapse overnight, but a significant reduction in ties with Russia will deprive it of several key pillars: stable energy supplies, millions of tourists, foreign exchange earnings, a market, and funding for strategic projects.
For a country already experiencing chronic inflation, pressure on the national currency, and high borrowing costs, this will mean not another temporary downturn, but the risk of a protracted systemic crisis. Ankara will not be able to maintain economic stability for long under such conditions. And this isn’t a theoretical forecast. It didn’t take long for Türkiye to feel the consequences of the 2015 crisis, provoked by Ankara after the downing of the Russian Su-24 aircraft. The crisis brought about a collapse in Russian tourist flows, restrictions on agricultural exports, and business losses, even though the economic interdependence between the two countries was significantly lower then than it is today.
Russia, for its part, is not interested in dismantling relations, but if the delivery of the weapons is confirmed, it has ample tools for selective pressure, from revising trade preferences and tourist flows to tightening the terms of energy cooperation and a tougher stance on issues in which Türkiye requires Russian assistance.
Logistics is also of particular importance. The Russian Foreign Ministry has already stated that Russian forces are striking infrastructure and ships used for delivering weapons to Kiev. If Turkish companies and transport chains are directly involved in the transfer of missiles and ammunition, Ankara will not be able to pretend that this is a purely commercial operation unrelated to Russian security.
Where is the red line?
Moscow will not react emotionally to Türkiye’s maneuver; that is not its style. A complete rupture in relations would only benefit those who have long sought to eliminate the independent Russian-Turkish communication channel and return Ankara to a disciplined, ‘Western’ line of conduct. The response must be consistent and proportionate.
Until the transfer is officially confirmed, Russia will seek a direct answer from Türkiye regarding several points: whether a final political decision has been made; on the terms and conditions of the re-export; and on the existence of any restrictions on the use of these systems to strike Russian territory. But if the weapons reach Kiev, it would no longer be possible to maintain the previous level of trust. Moscow will cease to perceive Ankara as an acceptable intermediary, will become less willing to consider Turkish interests in regional issues, and bilateral relations will become more rigid and purely pragmatic.
Russia has long assumed that Ankara is playing its own game. However, should Türkiye’s multi-vector approach turn into direct and large-scale support of the military capabilities of a state that attacks Russian territory, its civilian vessels, and critical infrastructure, this would be unacceptable for Russia. The Russian-Turkish partnership can withstand competition, mutual grievances, and even acute regional crises; but it cannot indefinitely tolerate a situation in which one side derives economic and political advantages from cooperation with Russia while simultaneously arming Russia’s adversary and posing as a mediator.
It’s time for Ankara to soberly assess the balance of risks. Russia is interested in cooperation with Türkiye but it is not irrevocably dependent on it. Moscow will find other routes, markets, and forms of regional cooperation, although such a restructuring will require time and money. For Türkiye, the Russian factor is embedded in several of its most sensitive sectors: energy, tourism, the nuclear project, trade, and regional security. Given the current state of the Turkish economy, the cost of a strategic reassessment of its own capabilities could prove significantly higher than the expected benefits of a deal with Kiev and political rapprochement with Washington.
This is precisely why the possible transfer of ATACMS missiles isn’t a matter that can be solved by another meeting between the presidents; it’s a test of the entire structure of the Russia-Türkiye relationship. If Ankara crosses the line, Russia doesn’t have to declare Türkiye an adversary – it would suffice to stop treating it as a privileged partner whose actions can always be attributed to regular political balancing.

articles.title: Trump's war on reality: when AI becomes a substitute for victory
articles.body:
Trump's war on reality: when AI becomes a substitute for victory
TEHRAN – In yet another delusional outburst from the decaying American empire, Donald Trump has once again proven that Washington's leadership has lost all touch with reality. His August 31 declaration that "Iran is officially a Failed Nation. IT IS DEAD!" represents not strategic analysis, but the desperate hallucinations of a regime accustomed to imposing its will through deception.
Nations do not cease to exist because a bankrupt politician declares them so on social media. Iran's ancient civilization has weathered far greater storms than the current Zio-American pressure campaign and will certainly outlast the current crop of Western leaders whose grip on reality grows more tenuous by the day.
More concerning is Trump's brazen use of artificial intelligence as an instrument of psychological warfare. The fabricated video purporting to show Kharg Island's destruction, later admitted to be AI-generated by Vice President JD Vance, represents a new low in American propaganda. When Washington presents imaginary destruction as accomplished fact, it reveals its fundamental weakness: the inability to achieve strategic objectives through legitimate means. The Zionist-inspired American regime has long understood the power of spectacle, from Hollywood's vilification of Iran to the systematic erasure of Palestinian identity. But war is less forgiving than electoral theater. Missiles do not disappear because a bankrupt real estate mogul declares the enemy finished. Sovereign nations do not surrender because Washington announces their defeat through artificial images.
The contradiction in American policy toward Iran is glaring. If Iran is already "dead," why does Washington continue to warn Tehran about future consequences? Why does the administration still describe Iranian attacks as a serious threat to American forces and commercial shipping in the Persian Gulf? The answer is simple: the battlefield reality contradicts the propaganda. Iran has not only survived Washington's maximum pressure campaign but has demonstrated remarkable resilience. Despite facing the most comprehensive economic warfare in modern history, Iran continues to advance its scientific capabilities, maintain regional influence, and defend its sovereignty. Iran's military capabilities remain formidable, as evidenced by the embarrassing failures of American and Israeli operations against Iranian assets. The Islamic Republic's air defense systems, naval presence in the strategic Persian Gulf, and missile capabilities continue to pose a genuine deterrent to Zionist ambitions in the region.
One cannot separate Washington's hostility toward Iran from the corrosive influence of the Zionist lobby on American foreign policy. The relentless push for confrontation serves Tel Aviv's interests far more than America's. Why should American soldiers sacrifice their lives for Israeli security? Why should American taxpayers fund endless conflicts that only benefit the apartheid regime in occupied Palestine? The Iranian people have repeatedly demonstrated their capacity to resist foreign domination. From the 1979 Islamic Revolution to the present, Iran has consistently rejected Western attempts to impose its will. The American war of words against Iran is fundamentally a war against national sovereignty and the right to chart one's own destiny free from imperial interference.
Perhaps most disturbing is Washington's callous exploitation of human suffering. Reported casualty figures from American sources have shifted dramatically from tens of thousands to more than 100,000 alleged deaths with little evidence to support these claims. If accurate, these figures represent a humanitarian catastrophe demanding independent verification. If inaccurate, their use as political slogans reduces human tragedy to mere ammunition in Washington's propaganda war. The Islamic Republic has repeatedly called for international investigations into American and Israeli war crimes, including the systematic assassination of Iranian scientists, cyberattacks on civilian infrastructure, and economic warfare that constitutes collective punishment under international humanitarian law.
Washington's reckless rhetoric also threatens the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most strategically important waterways. Any serious confrontation in the Persian Gulf would have devastating consequences for regional security and the global economy. These realities cannot be managed through memes, AI-generated videos, or declarations that an entire nation is "dead." The Islamic Republic has consistently demonstrated its commitment to regional stability, unlike the American regime that has left a trail of destruction from Afghanistan to Libya to Yemen.
When political leaders become more invested in declaring victory than establishing facts, credibility becomes collateral damage. The United States' strategic asset should be its credibility, yet every false image or exaggerated claim weakens this foundation. Propaganda can shape perception, but perception cannot substitute for strategy. AI can manufacture the image of a destroyed island. Social media can manufacture the appearance of triumph. None of it can manufacture victory. Military power can destroy infrastructure, but it cannot, by itself, manufacture political outcomes. This is a lesson America learned in Vietnam, Afghanistan, and Iraq, and will inevitably learn in its confrontation with Iran.
While Washington indulges in fantasies of Iranian collapse, the Islamic Republic continues to demonstrate remarkable resilience. Iran has transformed challenges into opportunities for self-reliance and technological advancement, from nuclear technology to biotechnology, from aerospace to nanotechnology. Iran's political system, grounded in Islamic values and republican institutions, has proven its legitimacy through successive elections and popular participation. The American claim that Iran is a "failed state" ignores the reality of a functioning government that provides services to its citizens, maintains security across its vast territory, and continues to exert influence from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean.
The broader issue extends far beyond Iran. The American empire is in terminal decline, unable to accept that the unipolar moment has passed. Washington's desperate attempts to maintain global hegemony through sanctions and military threats reflect not strength but weakness. China, Russia, and the emerging multipolar order represent a future that respects national sovereignty and cultural diversity. Iran will continue strengthening its ties with these powers, reducing its vulnerability to American pressure. The so-called "America First" policy reveals itself as "America Alone," isolated from the global consensus that rejects unilateralism.
Trump may dominate the news cycle with a post. He may make an artificial image trend across social media. None of that changes the battlefield reality.
Iran will continue its path of dignity, resistance, and development. The Islamic Republic will survive American propaganda, Zionist ambitions, and imperial pressures. Iranian civilization has endured for millennia; it will not collapse because a bankrupt American politician declares it "dead" on social media. The American empire, meanwhile, continues its inevitable decline, hoisted by its own petard of deception and moral bankruptcy. History will judge which civilization truly failed.

articles.title: Faith in fakes: How anti-Russian hysteria is driving the EU’s drone hoax
articles.body:
Faith in fakes: How anti-Russian hysteria is driving the EU’s drone hoax
Is it a bird? Is it a plane? Is it a well-timed ploy to ramp up defense spending? The late-autumn drone sighting hysteria that swept across Norway, Denmark, the Netherlands and Belgium, was used by the bloc to amplify and entrench an anti-Russia stance that has seen it throw hundreds of billions it cannot afford into weapons and a war its chosen side cannot win.
Tens of millions of Euro has since been spent on the back of a 'scare' that has been shown to have been irrational, exuberant and driven by vested interests.
The most bizarre national security scare in recent European history began at Copenhagen’s Kastrup Airport on September 2 last year. According to Denmark’s Frihedsbrevet news site, an airport employee told her supervisors that she saw two drones approach the area “stealthily,” adding that “they are big. They are not toys.”
The airport was temporarily shut down, and within hours, reports of a similar drone incursion came in from Oslo, Norway.
“I can only say that this is in my eyes a serious attack on Danish critical infrastructure,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said at the time. “I cannot in any way deny that it is Russia.” Her Norwegian counterpart, Gahr Store, came to a similar conclusion. “Russia has violated Norwegian airspace on three occasions this spring and summer,” he claimed. “We cannot determine whether this was done intentionally or due to navigation errors. Regardless of the cause, this is not acceptable.”
“It is clear we are witnessing a pattern of persistent contestation at our borders,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said. “Our critical infrastructure is at risk. And Europe will respond to this threat with strength and determination.”
Open-source investigators insisted that the sightings were a hoax from the outset. Sleuths on the Metabunk forums concluded that the ‘drone’ seen at Kastrup Airport in the above footage was actually a small single-engine plane. FlightRadar24 data showed one such plane – a Socata TB-20 Trinidad – passing over the airport’s main runway twice at the time of the sighting.
Where were drones spotted?
Nevertheless, panic spread across northern Europe as drones were supposedly spotted at the following airports, military bases, and infrastructure sites in the following days and weeks:
- September 23: Aalborg Airport, Denmark
- September 24: Aalborg Airport, Billund Airport, Sonderborg, Esbjerg and Skrydstrup airports, Denmark
- September 25: Billund Airport, Denmark; Thyssenkrupp factory, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany; University Medical Center, Kiel, Germany; Bundeswehr base, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Germany
September 26: Karup Air Base, Skrydstrup Air Base, Jutland Dragoon Regiment base, Denmark
- September 27: Orland Main Air Station, Norway
- September 28: Bronnoysund Airport, Norway; Borris Camp, Denmark
- October 2: Munich Airport, Germany; Elsenborn-Butgenbach Air Base, Belgium
- October 3: Munich Airport, Germany
- October 31: Berlin-Brandenburg Airport, Germany
- November 2: Bremen Airport, Germany; Kleine Brogel Air Base, Belgium
- November 6: Gothenburg Airport, Sweden; Brussels Airport, Antwerp Port, Belgium
- November 9: Liege Airport, Doel Nuclear Power Plant, Belgium
- November 22: Volkel Air Base, Netherlands
- December 1: In the Irish Sea off Dublin, during Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s arrival by plane
Police across northern Europe received thousands of additional drone reports from civilians. In Denmark alone, nearly 6,000 reports of suspected drones were filed.
Did the drones even exist?
Not only is there no proof that Russia was connected with these sightings, there is no evidence that any drones were present at all. No wreckage has been recovered, no perpetrators have been identified, and no footage of the drones exists, except for the video from Copenhagen that apparently shows a light aircraft.
Despite being certain that Denmark was under “hybrid attack,” Mette Frederiksen acknowledged in late September that there could be an “alternate explanation” for the sightings. Six months later, six government sources told Denmark’s TV2 that they don’t “have any technical evidence to support that Denmark was subjected to a hybrid attack with drones.” Frihedsbrevet’s sources came to a similar conclusion, with the airport employee who reported the initial sighting admitting that she could have been mistaken.
Airport management still insist that drones were present in the area on September 22, but police have not acknowledged any drones, only “reports” of drones.
Danish troops reportedly opened fire on a drone over Borris Camp on September 28. According to an investigation by TV2, the only aircraft operating in the area at the time was a turboprop passenger plane. The Danish military, if TV2’s reporting is correct, nearly shot down a civilian aircraft over a false alarm.
After interviewing witnesses and reviewing surveillance footage, Norwegian police closed their investigation on November 6, stating that they were “unable to confirm or deny whether drones were actually observed on the night of September 23.”
German police have not been able to confirm any drone activity; Dutch officials have identified no threat, with internal documents stating that there was “no indication of sabotage or attacks on vital objects.” Dutch and Belgian authorities have found no credible basis for panic, with Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken issuing a half-apology last month for attempting to pass off a video of a police helicopter as evidence of nefarious aerial activity.
Did they just lie?
Out of every country involved, Denmark’s leaders were most insistent that Russia was behind the spate of sightings. Frederiksen, Defense Minister Troels Lund Poulsen, and Justice Minister Peter Hummelgaard all described the incidents as “attacks,” despite nothing being attacked and no attackers being present.
“I consider it a new reality that Denmark and Europe are under more violent and frequent hybrid attacks,” Frederiksen said in a televised address on September 25. “And even though the authorities cannot conclude who is behind the hybrid attacks…there is primarily one country that poses a threat to Europe's security – and that is Russia.”
The flood of tips and reports from the public can be written off either as mass hysteria, or – more charitably – as a natural reaction from Europeans primed by their politicians and media to believe that Russia is planning an all-out war on the continent. As for why Frederiksen would stoke this fear, however, some clues can be found in her actions.
At the time, Denmark was just over a year into an historic rearmament program. After a €5.4 billion military budget hike in 2024, Frederiksen announced last February that defense spending would be increased from 2.4% to 3% of GDP by 2030 (since increased to 3.5%). By late 2025, Denmark had purchased hundreds of armored combat vehicles, signed contracts for new air defense systems, increased annual conscription numbers, and, for the first time in its history, introduced compulsory military service for women.
Denmark, she said last February, needs to undergo a “massive rearmament,” because “We don’t know what [Russian President Vladimir Putin] is planning, but we know that he and Russia are in the process of rearming.”
Frederiksen referenced this rearmament again in her September address, declaring that “the events of recent days only emphasize how important it is.”
Denmark held the EU’s rotating presidency at the time, and Frederiksen added that the alleged drone threat would be made front and center when EU leaders met in Copenhagen the following week, and that she would push for “the establishment of an actual drone wall.”
The EU’s drone wall
Frederiksen kept her word. Published on October 16, the European Commission’s ‘Defense Readiness Roadmap’ stated that a ‘European Drone Defense Initiative’ – the so-called “drone wall” comprising sensors and interceptors – would be operational along the bloc’s eastern borders with Russia and Belarus by 2027.
🚨🇪🇺 “We need to act now”Ursula von der Leyen now wants to build a “Drone Wall” on the Eastern Flank of Europe to protect from the alleged Russian Aggression. pic.twitter.com/UAGH93fKRc
— Concerned Citizen (@BGatesIsaPyscho) October 1, 2025
Drones continued to dominate the agenda at a European Council summit in Brussels in December. “The European Council strongly condemns all recent hybrid attacks against the European Union and its Member States,” read a statement released after the meeting. “In the light of Russia’s and Belarus’ intensified hybrid campaign, it calls for accelerated efforts to strengthen resilience, protect critical infrastructure, and…decisively ramp up Europe’s defense readiness by 2030.”
None of this is to suggest that Denmark orchestrated the drone panic to justify its remilitarization, or to sell the EU’s “drone wall.” Both initiatives were already underway at the time. Instead, it illustrates how Danish and EU officials saw an opportunity not to let a crisis go to waste, and kept the drone threat alive even as their own police forces, to put it mildly, struggled to substantiate it.
Belgium's very own drone crisis
Frederiksen wasn’t the only national leader who saw an opportunity amid the panic. Remember Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken? After police hotlines were flooded with more than 550 reports of drones between September and December, Francken bypassed the standard bidding process to authorize the purchase of €50 million worth of drone detection and jamming systems.
An investigation by Belgium’s VRT broadcaster has since found that none of the reports of drones were credible, and Francken has been hammered by the opposition for sharing an image of a ‘drone’ over Brussels Airport that turned out to be a police helicopter. VRT found that the defense ministry ignored warnings from Belgium’s Inspectorate of Finance and purchased detection antennas at an inflated price, and Francken is now the subject of an inquiry by the Brussels Public Prosecutor's Office.
The debacle is reminiscent of the Agusta-Dassault affair. During the 1980s, defense contractors Agusta and Dassault paid the equivalent of €4 million in bribes to secure no-bid contracts for AW109 transport helicopters and electronic warfare equipment. Once exposed, the scandal led to the criminal conviction of Belgian Defense Minister Guy Coeme and Foreign Minister and NATO Secretary General Willy Claes.
So did Russian drones spook the EU?
Nearly eight months after the first ‘drones’ were spotted over Copenhagen, the crisis is still being milked across Europe. In early May, long after the threat had been debunked in Denmark, Norway, Belgium, and the Netherlands, the Dutch defense ministry announced that it would acquire approximately 900 “electro-optical aiming devices” for use against UAVs, “without prior announcement due to the urgency of a crisis situation.”
Questioned by the Belgian parliament in April, Francken insisted that there is “no other plausible explanation” for the reports other than Russian drones, and that the only way to prove or disprove this is to invest in drone defense technology. “As long as you don’t have the means to detect and neutralize drones, it stands to reason that you cannot immediately produce physical evidence,” he told lawmakers.
The Dutch and Belgians aren’t letting a lack of evidence stop them from pursuing the defense deals that they wanted from this crisis, and the EU is unlikely to step in and pump the brakes.
The EU's censorious and paranoid media industry is the perfect environment for fake news to fester, as long as it suits the bloc. Remember, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's claims of “GPS jamming” hitting her plane on a trip to Bulgaria last September, and how, despite it being roundly debunked within days, it has been allowed to fester to serve her political agenda.
Anti-Russian hysteria is the animating political force in the EU, and the bloc’s leaders clearly aren’t going to let police and media investigations, or common sense, put a stop to the show.

articles.title: China assured Finland it would not allow Russia to use nuclear weapons – Finnish president
articles.body:
China assured Finland it would not allow Russia to use nuclear weapons – Finnish president
Finnish President Alexander Stubb said this in an interview with Politico, Ukrinform reports.
Asked whether Russia could use nuclear weapons, Stubb dismissed the possibility, saying Beijing was helping to “rein in” the escalation of Russia’s war against Ukraine.
“This summer, China’s foreign minister came to visit me, and I raised this issue. He replied, ‘We will never allow this to happen.’ And I think that is quite an effective deterrent,” Stubb said.
Read also: Pressure must be put on the entire coalition supporting Russia to achieve peace – expert
On July 5, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met with Stubb in Helsinki. Among other issues, they discussed Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and European security. China remains one of Moscow’s most important economic and diplomatic partners.
Stubb also stressed that Moscow benefits when Europeans focus on the prospect of nuclear escalation or a direct attack on NATO.
“Russia wants us Europeans to sit here and discuss: Will Russia escalate? Will Russia use nuclear weapons? Will Russia attack NATO and Europe?” the Finnish president said.
His advice on the matter was characteristically restrained: “Stay calm, keep your cool, remain composed, stay vigilant. Don’t dramatize it. Prepare for the worst so that we can avoid it.”
In the interview, Stubb also played down concerns about an imminent Russian attack on NATO, saying Moscow was more likely to be “provoking” the alliance to test its response than preparing for war. According to Stubb, Russian troops remain in Ukraine, while NATO’s deterrence makes a direct attack on the alliance highly unlikely.
At the same time, the Finnish president said he believed Europe was approaching the point when it would be useful to resume direct political dialogue with Moscow.
“I am convinced that we are approaching the day when it would be useful for Europeans to establish more direct contact with Russia,” he said. “Especially because we need to avoid misunderstandings.”
Europe “has not reached that point yet,” Stubb stressed, noting that supporting Ukraine remains the immediate priority.
“You can’t just press the ‘mute’ button. You have to start a discussion,” he added.
As reported, amid threats from Russia, NATO is working on plans to expand nuclear deterrence in Europe, with one of the options under consideration being the deployment of additional U.S. nuclear warheads.

articles.title: Has Trump entered a dangerous nuclear game?
articles.body:
Donald Trump's recent remarks about the possibility of using weapons of mass destruction have once again raised a discussion that goes beyond the usual political disputes between Tehran and Washington; an issue that has faced serious reactions even inside America. In this context, Tucker Carlson, the well-known American journalist and host, referring to Trump's statements about the use of nuclear weapons, said these remarks mean crossing a red line. He stressed that any political official who raises the first use of nuclear weapons has lost the qualification to continue leading, and Trump should be removed from power immediately.
The importance of these remarks is not merely in Carlson's personal position. What matters is the reopening of a discussion that over the past decades has been recognized, even among America's opponents and rivals, as one of the most dangerous red lines of Washington's security policy: Can an American president raise the use of nuclear weapons as part of the tools of pressure in a regional crisis, without this threat leading to broad strategic consequences?
The issue is not just a threat.
Trump had previously, during political pressures against Iran, used rhetoric that significantly raised the level of threat. At one point, he said that if Iran did not reach an agreement with America within the specified deadline, "an entire civilization" might be destroyed. Of course, Trump later ruled out the use of nuclear weapons against Iran and stressed that America does not need such weapons.
But in international politics, the distance between "threat," "bluff," and "real decision" is never clear enough that one can simply pass over it. A threat becomes dangerous when the other side is forced to factor the probability of its realization into its calculations.
Regarding Iran, this issue has double importance. The Islamic Republic has shown over the past years that under military pressure and threat, it does not necessarily move toward accepting the other side's demands. In some cases, America's maximum threats, when faced with real and significant costs for Washington, have led to retreat or a change of position.
From this perspective, part of what Trump pursues as the policy of "maximum pressure" has a fundamental problem: a threat is effective when it has credibility. If a threat is repeated too often but does not achieve the expected result in practice, it not only loses its deterrent power but can also lead to the weakening of the threatener's credibility.
In analyzing Iran's behavior, one should not look merely at military power or the number of missiles and drones. The main issue is the formation of a kind of mutual deterrence.
America has a very high destructive power, but military power alone does not mean the ability to impose a political outcome. The experience of past years in the Middle East has shown that the destruction of certain military targets and achieving a stable political end are two completely different matters.
Iran is also trying precisely at this point to increase the cost of America's military decision. Tehran knows that it cannot match America in terms of the volume of military capability, but it can change the cost-benefit calculation of Washington's decision.
This is where the concept of deterrence finds meaning. Deterrence does not necessarily mean that a country can defeat the other side; rather, it is enough for it to make the other side understand that military victory does not necessarily mean political victory.
Therefore, when Trump speaks of destroying a country or even a civilization, the issue is not just the intensity of his rhetoric. The more important question is whether Washington is truly prepared to pay the political, economic, security, and regional costs of such a decision.
Tucker Carlson's reaction should also be seen within this same framework. He is among the figures who have repeatedly warned in recent years about America's military interventionism and the expansion of foreign wars.
Therefore, his objection is not merely a political disagreement with Trump. Behind this objection lies a deeper concern: if the use of nuclear weapons becomes a normal option in American foreign policy, then the issue will no longer be just Iran. Other countries will also receive the message that security guarantees, the rules of deterrence, and even the boundaries of the use of nuclear weapons may be affected by the decision of a president.
This issue can create a chain effect. Countries that feel vulnerable vis-à-vis great powers may seek to build independent deterrence capability more than before. In such circumstances, instead of reducing the nuclear threat, a race for building greater deterrence will begin.
Perhaps the most important part of the matter is this. The post-Cold War world had tried to preserve the use of nuclear weapons as an exceptional option and the last tool of deterrence. But the more this rhetoric is repeated in everyday political disputes, the more the boundary between "threat for deterrence" and "threat for actual use" becomes blurred.
This trend is dangerous for America as well. Washington's power does not depend only on its aircraft carriers, fighter jets, and nuclear arsenal; an important part of America's power stems from its political credibility and the trust of its allies.
If America's allies feel that Washington's decisions could drag them into wars whose control has slipped away, it is natural that they will seek more independent options. For this reason, a nuclear threat may appear to be a sign of strength, but in the long term it can be a sign of a crisis in the management of power.
However, everything should not be reduced to the person of Trump. Trump may speak more bluntly, more aggressively, and more unpredictably than many American presidents, but the problems that American foreign policy faces today existed before him as well.
The main issue is the gap between America's military power and its ability to convert this power into sustainable political results. Washington can still target objectives in various parts of the world, but the question is what happens after the attack? Does the other side surrender? Do America's allies stand by it? Does domestic public opinion accept the cost of war? And most importantly, can America stop the war at the point it wants?
Ultimately, perhaps the most important message of Carlson's remarks is that even inside America, a serious disagreement has formed about the boundaries of the use of military power. Iran and the United States may confront each other in various arenas, but it should not be forgotten that every time the rhetoric of nuclear threat enters this dispute, the scope of danger extends beyond the two countries. The issue is no longer just what Trump says or how Iran responds; the issue is that if nuclear threat becomes a normal part of the language of foreign policy, who can guarantee that one day it will not cross the line from threat?
MNA

articles.title: NATO and EU Press Spain and Greece to Send Expiring Patriot Missiles to Ukraine
articles.body:

NATO and EU Press Spain and Greece to Send Expiring Patriot Missiles to Ukraine
NATO and European Union countries are urging Spain and Greece to provide Ukraine with Patriot interceptor missiles, focusing on PAC-2 stocks that are approaching the end of their shelf life.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Bloomberg on September 1, the requests were made over the summer as Ukraine faces growing demand for air defense interceptors amid intensified Russian missile strikes. One option under discussion would see Norway purchase the missiles from Spain and Greece before transferring them to Ukraine.
The issue is expected to be discussed during meetings of EU defense and foreign ministers in Ireland on September 1 and 2. Representatives from Ukraine, the UK, Norway, Iceland, and Switzerland are also participating.
“The main issue is air defense,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said ahead of the meetings on September 1, adding that Ukraine is “lacking interceptors.”
Spain and Greece hold some of the largest Patriot missile reserves among Ukraine’s partners, according to Bloomberg. Allied governments are particularly interested in their PAC-2 interceptors, some of which are nearing the end of their designated shelf life.
“We know that some of the countries have interceptors that will expire soon,” Kallas said. “So it would be very good if those would be given to Ukraine.”
Greece has previously supplied ammunition to Ukraine but has resisted requests to transfer Patriot assets, citing its own defense requirements and its longstanding tensions with Türkiye.
Spain, meanwhile, has pledged €1 billion ($1.2 billion) in military assistance to Ukraine in 2026. A Spanish Defense Ministry official and a Greek government spokesperson declined to comment to Bloomberg on the latest discussions.
Bloomberg reported that Ukraine’s allies are looking for additional sources of Patriot interceptors as existing stocks come under pressure and manufacturing new missiles requires significant lead time. Demand for the US-made air defense system has also increased due to the ongoing war with Iran.
Additional air defense supplies are expected to reach Ukraine through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), which allows NATO allies to finance purchases of US weapons for Kyiv.
The discussions come as Ukraine continues to seek additional Patriot ammunition to defend against Russian ballistic missile attacks. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that securing sufficient interceptor stocks for the coming winter remains one of Ukraine’s key defense priorities.

articles.title: Agenstvo: CIA director traveled to Moscow to urge peace talks. Putin planned to meet him but changed his mind.
articles.body:
Agenstvo: CIA director traveled to Moscow to urge peace talks. Putin planned to meet him but changed his mind.
Vladimir Putin had planned to meet with CIA Director John Ratcliffe during his August 25 visit to Moscow but called it off after learning the purpose of the trip, a source close to the Kremlin told the independent Russian investigative outlet Agentstvo.
According to the source, Ratcliffe urged Russian leadership to reach a deal to end the war with Ukraine as soon as possible, arguing that Russia’s military and economic situation is deteriorating and that the Kremlin would be better off striking a deal now rather than waiting to weaken further.
Ratcliffe met with Sergey Naryshkin, head of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), and Alexander Bortnikov, head of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), according to Western media. The substance of one of those conversations reached Putin, prompting the Kremlin to call off his personal meeting with Ratcliffe — a meeting Putin had initially cleared his schedule to hold.
The New York Times previously reported that Ratcliffe shared with Bortnikov his “bleak assessment” of Russia’s position in the war with Ukraine and called for peace talks to begin.
The Agentstvo source said the CIA director’s message sounded as though “Volodymyr Zelensky is already standing on Poklonnaya Hill, looking at the Kremlin through binoculars.” “Everyone understands that’s not the case. It seems Ratcliffe got the wrong address,” he added.
It remains unclear whether the CIA director’s position on the Russia–Ukraine war reflected the view of the White House as a whole.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow marked the first trip by the head of the American intelligence agency to Russia since the start of the full-scale war. The visit was unannounced and conducted in secrecy.
The Kremlin announced that Putin did not meet with Ratcliffe, though the American official spoke with representatives of Russia’s intelligence agencies.
Western media have offered several theories about the purpose of the CIA director’s visit, from urging the start of peace talks and warning against an attack on NATO countries to calling for reduced cooperation with Iran.
According to the American news outlet Axios, Ratcliffe also proposed a meeting of the presidents of the United States, Russia, and Ukraine. The Kremlin stated that such a meeting would only be possible to “finalize agreements.”
