Indian Citizen Among 12 Killed as Russia Pounds Kyiv and Ukraine With Ballistic Missiles, Drones
An Indian citizen was among 12 people killed as Russia unleashed ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones across Ukraine overnight, striking homes, a Kyiv railway depot, businesses and critical infrastructure.
An Indian citizen was among 12 people killed in a massive Russian missile and drone barrage across Ukraine, with strikes hitting apartment buildings, a Kyiv railway depot, businesses and critical infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on September 1.
Dozens more were injured as Russia deployed large numbers of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles against Kyiv and several other regions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“In many cities and communities, work to address the aftermath of the Russian attack has been ongoing since last night—nearly 350 first responders are involved in Kyiv and the region alone. A significant number of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles were used in the attack,” Zelenskyy said.
He added that residential buildings and civilian infrastructure were among the sites hit.
“Unfortunately, residential buildings and civilian infrastructure have been damaged,” the Ukrainian leader stated.
Boryspil, east of Kyiv, was among the hardest-hit cities. A five-story apartment building was damaged there, forcing emergency crews to evacuate 50 people. Businesses were also struck.
“In Boryspil, an ordinary five-story residential building was damaged. Fifty people were evacuated. All necessary services are on the ground. Businesses were also struck. Overall, 4 people were killed and 13 injured in the city. My condolences,” Zelenskyy said.
Kyiv itself suffered a deadly ballistic missile strike on railway infrastructure.
Russian forces deliberately targeted a railway depot and other railway facilities in the capital, according to Ukrzaliznytsia CEO Oleksandr Pertsovskyi.
Seven people were killed at the depot, six of them Ukrzaliznytsia employees. Another railway worker was hospitalized with injuries.
Dozens of employees survived because they had moved into shelters during the air raid alert.
The strike caused extensive destruction around the depot, including the complete destruction of a workshop, while emergency crews continued fighting several fires.
Rail traffic was temporarily suspended along two sections following the strike before service was restored.
“All of this is nothing compared with the terrible loss of our colleagues,” Pertsovskyi wrote, adding that the company was contacting the families of those killed and providing support.
Zelenskyy later confirmed the death toll at the railway facility.
“In Kyiv, a strike on a railway depot killed 7 people,” he said.
Russian strikes also continued against Odesa and the surrounding region, leaving thousands of households without electricity.
“Since last evening, guided aerial bomb and drone strikes have continued against Odesa and the region. Thousands of families were left without electricity, and work is ongoing to restore power to people as quickly as possible,” Zelenskyy stated.
Russia also damaged a border crossing with Romania and infrastructure used for Ukrainian exports.
“A border crossing with Romania was deliberately damaged, as was export infrastructure,” Zelenskyy said.
The Kherson, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, Chernihiv, Zhytomyr, Sumy and Dnipro regions also came under Russian strikes.
“Overall, 12 people were killed, among them an Indian citizen, and dozens more were injured in the attack. My condolences to everyone who has lost family and loved ones,” Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian leader said the casualty toll once again showed how strongly civilian survival depends on the availability of air defense systems.
“Russia always plans its strikes specifically to cause as much destruction to people’s lives as possible, and it succeeds only when air defense capabilities are insufficient,” Zelenskyy stated.
He called for increased deliveries of systems capable of intercepting ballistic missiles, particularly through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, or PURL, and bilateral assistance from Ukraine’s partners.
“I am grateful to everyone helping Ukraine receive anti-ballistic capabilities through PURL and bilateral supplies, and it is very important that these deliveries increase this fall,” Zelenskyy said.
He stressed that additional air defense support has an immediate impact on civilian casualties.
“The number of victims of Russian terror directly hinges on every new package of assistance. I thank everyone who is helping make Ukraine more resilient,” Zelenskyy added.
Previously, a large-scale aerial attack struck the city and region of Odesa, with local authorities reporting multiple explosions across the area.
The assault involved high-speed airborne targets, standard and jet-powered drones, loitering munitions, missiles, and guided aerial bombs launched from both northern directions and the Black Sea.

articles.title: Japan to Arm Fighter Jets with AARGM-ER Missiles to Counter Chinese Air Defenses
articles.body:
Japan’s Ministry of Defense will begin the procurement process for AARGM-ER anti-radiation missiles in 2027 to counter Chinese air defense systems.
This is indicated in the Japanese Ministry of Defense’s budget document for fiscal year 2027.
Following the establishment of Japan’s Air Self-Defense Force, the missile will become the first weapon of this class to be operated by the Japanese Air Self-Defense Force.
The procurement of these missiles is intended to enable their use from U.S.-made combat platforms, including the F-35, which Japan plans to operate for decades to come.
This comes amid increased Chinese military activity around Japan and the modernization of Japan’s air-launched weapons, which long remained predominantly defensive. This approach significantly limited the strike capabilities of Japanese combat aircraft.
The AARGM-ER (AGM-88G Advanced Anti-Radiation Guided Missile – Extended Range) is a next-generation U.S. air-launched anti-radiation missile designed primarily to detect, suppress, and destroy enemy air defense systems.
The missile is designed to engage not only fixed radar sites but also mobile surface-to-air missile systems, command posts, and other elements of an integrated air defense system.
One key feature is its ability to continue the engagement even after the adversary’s radar station has been switched off.
The missile uses a multi-mode guidance system that lets it detect and track a target after it stops radiating radar emissions.
The AARGM-ER was initially developed for the U.S. Navy’s F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and EA-18G Growler. The program was subsequently expanded to the F-35 family, including the F-35A, F-35B, and F-35C versions.
Militarnyi previously reported that the Japan Air Self-Defense Force had begun testing the F-2 fighter with a new long-range air-launched cruise missile.
The exact specifications of the air-launched variant are currently unknown.
Meanwhile, given that the ground-launched variant’s range is estimated at 1,200–1,500 km, the air-launched version will likely have similar performance, or potentially an even greater range, because it launches from an aircraft.

Russian forces attacked civilian infrastructure and residential buildings in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi, Holosiivskyi, and Solomianskyi districts overnight on September 1, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service reported.
The strikes killed eight people and injured five others, including three children, sparking fires and partially destroying a residential building.
Russian forces also struck railway infrastructure in Kyiv, including a depot, the state railway operator Ukrainian Railways reported. The strike killed seven people — six of them railway employees — and injured another company employee. Ukrainian media reported that the strike hit the city’s Darnytskyi district.
In the Kyiv region, a Russian strike using ballistic missiles and drones killed four people and injured 13, local authorities stated. The strike also damaged residential buildings, vehicles, and infrastructure, the State Emergency Service reported.
In Boryspil, the strike damaged a five-story residential building, two private houses, and a store, and hit an industrial building at another address in the city. Rescuers evacuated 48 people.
Russian drones attacked the Orlivka ferry crossing on the border between Ukraine’s Odesa region and Romania, Ukrainian border guards reported. The crossing has since suspended operations.
In the Odesa region, a massive Russian strike damaged residential buildings and sparked a fire at a sewing workshop, injuring one person, local authorities stated.
Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed its forces struck military enterprises and energy facilities in Kyiv and the surrounding region, as well as infrastructure in Odesa, the Odesa region, and the ports of Odesa and Chornomorsk.

articles.title: Trump threatens to ‘hit Iran hard’ after new flare-up
articles.body:
Trump threatens to ‘hit Iran hard’ after new flare-up
US President Donald Trump has vowed to “hit Iran hard” following Tehran’s retaliatory strikes on US military installations in Jordan, raising the prospect of another round of escalation after a month-long lull in direct fighting.
Iran fired ballistic missiles and drones at US military positions after US forces struck Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said its attack targeted the King Hussein and Al-Azraq air bases in Jordan in retaliation for the US strike, which Tehran said killed two Iranian soldiers and a civilian and injured several others.
“There will be a response,” Trump told Fox News reporter Trey Yingst by phone on Monday. “We’re going to hit them hard.”
Jordan said its air defenses intercepted eight missiles that entered its airspace, with no damage officially reported on the ground. Trump claimed that US forces allowed one incoming missile to pass through their defenses after determining that it was not going to hit anything “significant.”
Despite threatening further military action, Trump suggested that negotiations remain possible. “They want to meet so badly,” he told Fox. “The sanctions are kicking in really strongly.”
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran is “not looking for war” but would deliver a “decisive response” to further attacks.
Trump and senior US officials were already considering a plan for periodic strikes on Iranian military capabilities around the Strait of Hormuz before the latest exchange, Axios reported, citing three US officials.
The proposal, developed by US Central Command and backed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, would target Iranian radar, air defenses, and anti-ship missile capabilities as they are rebuilt. One US official described the proposed approach as an effort to “mow the lawn.”
The renewed military threats come after the Trump administration shifted much of its pressure campaign toward economic measures, launching an “economic onslaught” against Iran’s trade partners under Operation Economic Outcast.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that Washington plans to roll out new secondary sanctions every week against foreign banks and companies that continue doing business with Iran, warning allies and rivals alike that they could be cut off from the US financial system.
“You’re either with us or you’re with the Iranians,” Bessent said, adding that Washington is prepared to use “financial violence if we have to.”

articles.title: Trump mulls resuming Iran war after first strikes in weeks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump mulls resuming Iran war after first exchange of fire in weeks
US President Donald Trump and his senior aides are considering resuming the war on Iran in a bid to prevent it from attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz , three US officials told Axios.
The report came several hours after Trump threatened to hit Iran "hard" after the two foes traded fire for the first time in over a month.
After six months of war, the foes remain at an impasse, with Iran keeping the strategic Strait of Hormuz closed and the US persisting with a naval counter-blockade of Iran.
According to Axios, the plan was drawn up US Central Command (CENTCOM) and is backed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. It would stop short of full-scale war in favour of limited strikes targeting Iranian missile and radar sites.
One official described the floated operation as "mowing the lawn", a popular term among Israeli military officials to describe the periodic bombing of Gaza.
"The President retains all options at his disposal. The Iranians want to make a deal, but they are always a day late and a dollar short," a White House official told the news outlet.
Late Sunday, the United States said it had carried out strikes on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran quickly retaliating by attacking US military targets in the Middle East.
The exchange raised fears of a return to major hostilities, with the US president vowing to respond.
"We're going to hit them hard," Trump said, according to a Fox News reporter who spoke to him briefly. "There will be a response."
The United States said it attacked Iranian rocket launchers on the island of Larak to prevent Tehran planting mines in the key shipping lane.
Iran responded by with missile and drone attacks aimed at Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, saying they targeted US forces there, but President Masoud Pezeshkian later on Monday called for dialogue.
"We continue to strive for a path of agreement and understanding, and we believe that continuing the war is neither in our interest, nor in the interest of the region," he said at a summit in Kyrgyzstan, adding "the solution to the existing problems is dialogue and cooperation".
State media reported that two people were killed in the US attack on Larak, with several others wounded.
Iran's powerful Revolutionary Guards, the ideological arm of its military, said the ballistic missile attack on two US air bases in Jordan caused "heavy damage".
Jordan's army said it had intercepted eight missiles, without stating their origin. Trump also told Fox that all the missiles fired at US forces had been shot down, except for one that was determined not to pose a threat.
Iran also said it targeted US personnel at an air base in the UAE and shot down an American drone over Hormuz.
Abu Dhabi said it intercepted a drone over the country's waters, but dismissed claims that Al Minhad Air Base had been targeted as "baseless".
The exchange of fire came after weeks of relative calm, with the Trump administration recently pivoting to "economic warfare".
Earlier on Monday, Trump had called Iran "a Failed Nation", saying on social media that its military was decimated, its finances were crumbling "and their leadership is in total disarray and incapable of properly representing the country".
Hormuz flashpoint
The two sides are still vying for control of the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran having blocked the passage of commercial ships since the war began, attacking vessels that seek to cross.
One-fifth of the world's oil passed through the strait before the war, which was triggered by a surprise wave of US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.
Despite traffic remaining throttled six months on, Trump has claimed the US navy has "total control" of the strait and has even called it US territory, with Washington last week announcing it had completed clearing explosives from the waterway.
Iran, however, insists it is in charge of the sealane. The Revolutionary Guards said Monday a "rogue" oil tanker caught fire near the strait after it hit two mines while attempting to transit an "illegal route".
The US military called the claim "disinformation", saying: "No ships have hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz."
Mediators have tried for months to broker an end to the war, but an earlier truce and memorandum of understanding fell apart.
Sporadic attacks resumed, but ultimately tapered off, with the US last striking Iran on 29 July, after having attacked Iran for 13 consecutive nights earlier that month.
With diplomacy stalled, Iran's foreign minister on Monday accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of tricking Washington into going to war.
"In Hebrew, Netanyahu openly crows that he suckered the US administration into a war on Iran on behalf of Israel," Abbas Araghchi wrote on X. "In English, he praises POTUS' leadership. Serpent."
(AFP and TNA staff)

articles.title: Russia attacked with ballistic and "Zircon" missiles; some of missiles and 187 of 218 drones neutralized
articles.body:
Russia attacked with ballistic and "Zircon" missiles; some of missiles and 187 of 218 drones neutralized
Kyiv • UNN
Russia launched 218 drones and missiles at Ukraine overnight, including ballistic missiles and "Zircon" missiles. Air defenses shot down or suppressed 199 targets.
Russia launched ballistic missiles, Zircon and other missiles, Banderoľ munitions, and 218 drones at Ukraine overnight; five ballistic missiles, two Banderoľ munitions, five Kalibr missiles, and 187 unmanned aerial vehicles were shot down or suppressed, while some missiles failed to reach their targets, the Ukrainian Air Force reported on Tuesday, UNN writes.
Details
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, during the night of September 1 (from 18:00 on August 31), the enemy attacked with:
-  Iskander-M/KN-23/S-400 ballistic missiles and Zircon anti-ship missiles from Russia’s Bryansk, Kursk, Voronezh, and Rostov regions; 
-  sea-launched Kalibr cruise missiles from Novorossiysk; 
-  Kh-31P anti-radiation missiles from the airspace over the Black Sea; 
-  S8000 Banderoľ munitions from Russia’s Bryansk region and from over the Sea of Azov; 
-  218 Shahed-type attack UAVs (about one-third of them jet-powered) and Parodya-type decoy drones from the following directions: Kursk, Millerovo, Orel, Primorsko-Akhtarsk – Russia, the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk region, and Hvardiiske – the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea. 
"The main directions of the attack were Odesa region and Kyiv region," the statement said.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, surface-to-air missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:30, air defenses had shot down/suppressed 199 targets: five Iskander-M/KN-23/S-400 ballistic missiles; two S8000 Banderoľ munitions; five Kalibr cruise missiles; and 187 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and drones of other types. Hits by enemy missiles and attack UAVs were recorded at 28 locations, as well as the falling of downed targets (debris) at 10 locations. In addition, some enemy missiles failed to reach their targets; information regarding their locations is being clarified. Unfortunately, there were deaths and injuries as a result of the Russian attack; we express our condolences to the families and loved ones...
The attack is ongoing; more than ten enemy UAVs are in the airspace.

articles.title: Ukrainian pilot details fight against jet-powered Shaheds
articles.body:
- A Ukrainian fighter pilot told Waypoint that jet-powered Shahed drones remain a difficult but viable target for crewed fighter jets despite the cost.
- He said Ukraine's main constraint is funding and procedural delays, not a failure of its layered air defense system.
A Ukrainian fighter pilot who runs the social media channel “Sonyashnyk” told the outlet Waypoint that jet-powered Shahed drones remain difficult to stop even as Ukraine’s air defense system continues to evolve, arguing that focus on the small number of drones that get through overlooks the far larger number destroyed before they reach populated areas.
The pilot, whose name was not disclosed, was asked where Ukraine’s air defense system fails most against jet-powered Shahed drones. He said no country’s air defense system could withstand the volume of daily Russian strikes, and pushed back on the idea that Ukraine’s system is failing.
“The amount of resources the enemy uses daily is colossal. Civilians focus on the number of targets that got through some echelon of our defense, but forget that downing enemy targets starts back over the swamps,” the pilot said.
He said Russia has adapted its tactics over the course of the war after realizing it could not overwhelm Ukraine’s defenses carelessly, now preparing major strikes with extensive resources and support from what he called allied “tyrants.” He said Russia has found gaps Ukraine currently lacks the means to close, including exploiting national borders and launching mass strikes during periods of worsening weather.
“In my opinion, our Achilles heel is funding, both from partners and locally. Many important initiatives and ideas have to pass through a hundred procedural councils before anyone hears them,” the pilot said. “As for allies, the world is still moving too slowly into World War III. That’s where the shortage of ammunition and other resources comes from.”
Asked whether it still makes sense to send crewed fighter jets after jet-powered Shaheds, given the cost involved, the pilot said the mission remains within a fighter jet’s core role of air dominance and integrated air defense work.
“From a fighter’s perspective it makes sense, because that’s literally our specialty: air dominance and working within the air defense system,” the pilot said. He said the older Geran-1 and Geran-2 drones had been a persistent nuisance for a period, but described the jet-powered Shahed as a comparatively good target given its flight characteristics.
“Financially it’s painful, but that’s our purpose,” he said. “In a single sortie even an old MiG can take out a dozen or so. You have to understand that since there aren’t many other options, you end up relying on skill and experience.” He added that some enemy targets fly at altitudes where cheaper interceptors simply cannot reach them or arrive in time.
Asked for two or three real priorities for countering jet-powered Shaheds systematically rather than case by case, the pilot said destroying the launch sites themselves is not realistic, since Russia can rebuild or relocate them, including launching from mobile platforms.
“Of course we need to conduct operations on enemy territory, hunt launch sites and logistics, factories and workshops,” he said. “But I also think that if all our forces are directed toward that alone, the enemy will simply move faster to operate from underground.” He said the more logical approach is parallel work: building out a layered, unified air defense system, even if unified only by sector or “line,” while continuously pressuring the enemy’s capabilities.
“If we’re given a sufficient quantity of interception means and expand the authority of commanders and leaders on the ground, then with competent coordination everything will be fine,” he said. He pointed to a shift he said Ukrainians witnessed roughly six months earlier, when, with sufficient interception resources available, only a pair of drones out of hundreds launched toward Kyiv managed to get through.

articles.title: Russian missile and drone attack on Kyiv kills at least eight
articles.body:
Russian missile and drone attack on Kyiv kills at least eight
A massive Russian missile and drone attack on Kyiv and its surrounding region killed at least eight people and wounded more than a dozen overnight, Ukrainian officials said Tuesday, as children prepared to return to school amid heightened fears of further strikes.
A "massive" Russian missile and drone attack on Kyiv and its surrounding areas killed at least eight and wounded more than a dozen others, Ukrainian officials said Tuesday.
The strikes came as children were set to return to school after the summer holidays, and as officials tightened security measures during fears of further Russian strikes.
"Kyiv region came under a massive attack by Russian missiles and strike drones tonight," Kyiv regional military administration chief Tymur Tkachenko said on Telegram.
AFP journalists in the capital heard around a dozen loud explosions and saw flashes in sky early Tuesday moments after the air force warned of incoming ballistic missiles.
"Sadly, 3 people were killed in the enemy attack on the capital," the city military admnistration said, adding that were reports of five wounded.
Strikes in Boryspil, east of Kyiv, damaged a business, leaving one person dead and another wounded, Tkachenko said, adding that eight more were wounded when a residential building was hit.
The Ukrainian air force had earlier warned that the threat of "ballistic weapons and other means of attack against Kyiv and the region remains in effect", and urged residents to remain in shelters.
Ukrainian children return to school on Tuesday, and the Kyiv regional military administration has warned there must be no large events in areas with a high level of risk.
Kyiv and its surrounding areas have come under sustained pressure from Russian drone attacks in recent weeks, with jet-powered drones adding to the threat and triggering as many as a dozen air-raid alerts a day.
One weekend attack on an ammunition depot killed 38 people in the capital's suburbs.
Both sides have escalated long-range strikes in recent months, targeting infrastructure such as warehouses, businesses, and oil and port facilities, as well as ships, increasing civilian casualties.
Ukraine faces a shortage of interceptor missiles, particularly US-made Patriot systems used against ballistic threats.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Scott Ritter: The CIA never comes to Russia in peace
articles.body:
Scott Ritter: The CIA never comes to Russia in peace
CIA Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow last week.
What we know: Ratcliffe met with Sergey Naryshkin, the director of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service. This has been confirmed by Naryshkin himself, who described the meeting as “routine.” We also know that the US spy chief did not meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“The meeting took place, there is nothing unusual in this,” Naryshkin stated afterwards. “In the practice of special services, meetings of managers, personal meetings or online are part of our work. So, the meeting with John Ratcliffe is a working format.”
Naryshkin refused to state what issues were discussed, explaining that they were within the competence of the intelligence services. “And the competence of the intelligence services is such a rather delicate and special thing,” the Russian spy chief said.
What we don’t know: literally anything else.
Rumors abound about additional attendees, as well as the agenda – or lack thereof – that was pursued by Ratcliffe during a meeting which appeared to be anything but routine. But the fact is, any meeting between Ratcliffe and Naryshkin, given the nature of the times we live in, could never be described as “routine.”
A quick reminder: John Ratcliffe’s CIA is currently at war with Russia. Literally.
Ratcliffe assumed his current position on January 23, 2025. Prior to this, he did a short stint as national intelligence director during the last year of Trump’s first term in office. He was a Texas congressman for a few years, as well as a small-town mayor and acting US attorney for the Eastern District of Texas.
He is a politician, not a spy.
But he is fully cognizant of the CIA’s secret war against Russia, having been fully briefed while serving as DNI. As a member of Congress, Ratcliffe was a leading policy maker on national security issues serving as a member of the House Intelligence and Homeland Security committees.
Any effort to portray him as some sort of “innocent abroad” fails on the face of the facts.
The CIA has always been at war with Russia. During the Cold War, Moscow Station (the name of the CIA’s operation center based out of the US Embassy) was literally the front line of the spy-versus-spy antics taking place between the US and the Soviet Union.
The CIA headed up Operation Cyclone, a massive paramilitary-driven effort to create a Vietnam-like quagmire for the Soviet Union in Afghanistan. The goal of Operation Cyclone was to kill Russians.
I worked with people who were directly or indirectly affiliated with Operation Cyclone. ‘Kill more Russians’ was literally their mantra.
There was a time when the CIA hired genuine Russia-area experts. The analysts who populated the Office of Soviet Analysis (SOVA) in the Directorate of Intelligence at the height of the Cold War were some of the best experts on the Soviet Union imaginable.
I know because I worked with them. From 1988-1990, I received two classified commendations from the director of the CIA for my analytical work involving the Soviet Union. I was considered by the CIA leadership to be a top-notch Soviet analyst.
In 1992 the CIA actively recruited me for an analytical position within the predecessor to SOVA, the Slavic and Eurasian Office. I was brought in for a high-level interview, after which I was informed that the CIA would be passing on my application. When I asked why, I was told that I was too married to old school thinking about Russia – in short, I was a ‘Sovietologist’.
The CIA was looking for people who could imagine Russia ‘differently’. What this meant was divorcing oneself from the mindset that Russia (i.e., the Soviet Union) was a peer-level opponent worthy of respect (my view), and instead adopting a stance that Russia was a defeated foe that needed to be kept down by any means necessary.
In the 1990s, the CIA’s task was to use Boris Yeltsin as an agent of influence to weaken Russia and facilitate foreign control over its resources. The CIA actively infiltrated every aspect of the Russian economy and used ‘soft power’ resources funded by the likes of the National Endowment for Democracy and overseen by the US Agency for International Development (USAID) to hijack Russian democratic institutions and Russian social life, especially through media-related activities.
The CIA also was very active in working to break Russia up into more manageable fiefdoms, each ruled over by a CIA-controlled lackey. The Russian-Chechen conflict was a primary example of this activity.
When Boris Yeltsin stepped aside in favor of Vladimir Putin as Russia’s president on New Year’s Eve 1999, the CIA immediately made it its task to undermine Putin and replace him with someone from the Yeltsin camp willing and able to do the CIA’s bidding.
Putin’s resistance and resilience as a Russian leader operating independent of CIA control helped shape a new generation of Russophobes in the United States. The first generation were the ‘new Russian’ thinkers that replaced the old school ‘Sovietologists’ at the end of the Cold War. To them, Russia was a playground for which to launch experiments on economic and political domination with absolutely zero regard to the price being paid by the people of Russia.
This generation of Russophobes simply detested Russia and the Russian people, failing to attribute any normative human value to their lives. Millions of Russians lost their lives as a result, and tens of millions of others suffered greatly.
Michael McFaul, the former US ambassador to Russia, falls into this category. So, too, does Fiona Hill. And Beth Sanner. People whose educational background and Russian experience pre-dates Putin, people who know the truth about Russia but opted instead to embrace the hegemonic policies of superpower singularity and work to weaken and destroy Russia.
But Putin’s stubborn hold on power, despite concerted efforts by the CIA to oust him (think Navalny), led to the birth of a new generation of Russophobes, so-called ‘experts’ whose only claim to relevance is their undying hatred of Putin and everything Russian.
It is this generation that has gravitated to the upper levels of the CIA’s analytical community, and who openly hate all things Russia. People like Andrea Kendall-Taylor and Julia Gurganus.
It is this openly Russophobic CIA that John Ratcliffe oversees.
His relationship with Julia Gurganus is both instructive and illustrative of the sickness that pervades the CIA when it comes to Russia. Gurganus was the National Intelligence Officer for Russia back in 2016-17, at the height of the Obama-era Russiagate scandal that tried to make the case of collusion between then-candidate Donald Trump and Russia to steal the 2016 presidential election from Hillary Clinton.
Gurganus helped manufacture the intelligence that underpinned this false allegation. She was a vociferous critic of Trump, so much so that the CIA quietly exiled her to a think tank position during Trump’s first term in office.
When Trump was reelected, Ratcliffe oversaw the whitewashing of Gurganus’ role in falsely accusing Trump of collusion, leading to the elevation of Gurganus as the senior CIA briefer onboard Air Force One as Trump flew to Alaska to meet with Putin in August 2025. That’s right – Ratcliffe purposefully cleansed Gurganus of her anti-Trump credentials so she could personally brief the president before his meeting with Putin.
Tulsi Gabbard, in her role as DNI, exposed Gurganus as an anti-Trump operative and had her security clearances revoked, but not before the damage was done.
There was a time when the CIA’s Directorate of Operations Russia House was home to living legends. People like Milton Beardon, who helped run Operation Cyclone and was chief of the Soviet/East European Division at the time the Soviet Union fell. Gardner Hathaway and Berton Gerber, who ran some of the most successful CIA spying operations from Moscow Station in the late 1970s and early 1980s.
And Murat Natirboff, another legendary Russian hand who led the Moscow Station during the Nicholas Daniloff affairs in the 1980s. Natirboff is instructional in this regard. His father was an officer in the Russian White Army which fought the Bolsheviks during the Russian Civil War. Natirboff hated the communists. But he loved Russia. He was held in very high regard by the Soviet officers of the KGB which faced off against him during his tour in Moscow.
I can personally attest to Murat’s feelings toward Russia – I met him after he left Moscow in 1988, where we spoke about my experiences in Votkinsk as an INF Treaty weapons inspector.
The CIA no longer employs people of this caliber in its operational work regarding Russia. Gone are the days of the Russian romantics – people who took the time to learn about their enemies to bring to life Sun Tzu’s classic observation: “If you know your enemy as yourself, you need not fear the outcome of a hundred battles.”
The present-day Directorate of Operations is overrun with paramilitary operatives, men (and women) who cut their teeth during the heyday of the post-9/11 ‘Global War on Terror’, where they oversaw secret wars in Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, and Iran.
They take their cue from veterans like Tom Sylvester, a former Navy SEAL who worked in the CIA’s Special Activities Branch as a Ground Branch operative. Tom headed the CIA’s efforts in Ukraine post-2022, when the Special Military Operation began. His job was literally to kill Russians.
People like ‘Santa Claus’, the nickname of the CIA’s Kiev Station Chief who sent Ground Branch to Ukraine post-2014 to train the Ukrainian intelligence special operations forces on how best to kill Russians.
Veterans of the CIA’s drone assassination programs now advise the Ukrainian drone operators on how to kill Russians and destroy Russian infrastructure.
In December 2025, the CIA helped direct Ukrainian drones toward a residence in Valdai where Putin was staying.
Yes – John Ratcliffe’s CIA tried to kill the Russian president. The CIA denies Putin was the target, but the data from the guidance chips extracted from Ukrainian drone debris appears to suggest otherwise.
Today, the CIA is knee-deep in the business of killing Russians. They continue to guide Ukraine’s expanded drone warfare campaign targeting Russia. And Russians.
This is John Ratcliffe. This is the organization he leads. So, when people reflect on the recent visit by Ratcliffe to Russia, never lose sight of his primary mission.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

Military
800 jet drones in four days: Russia is now firing type Ukraine's interceptors cannot catch. Of more than 1,500 drones launched over four days, about 800 have been jet-powered.
"In intercepts, they're screaming": Russia occupied this spit to control Ukraine's ports. Military says it has now isolated 2,500-strong grouping and destroyed all its artillery. Drone strikes and remote mining have cut supply, the Ukrainian soldiers say.

Ukrainian company builds single device that detects FPV drone, reads its video feed, and jams it. Brama has passed lab and combat testing and is now going through codification.
About $150 for airframe, about $875 for finished glider: Ukraine's BlueBird is selling its drone at every stage of assembly. Units pick the control system, camera, and electronics themselves; the bare airframe starts near $150.
International
Fired Ukrainian minister offers to help build America's drone army— for Patriot missiles in return. Mykhailo Fedorov is courting US investors for a fund that would build defense tech companies itself, not just back them.
The US built itself a Russo-Ukrainian drone-war drill—Poland is the first ally in. A Green Beret officer expects most of NATO's 32 members to want a look, as Ukraine's war experience reshapes how the alliance trains.
Russia's shadow war on Europe is widening—NATO still sees no attack coming. A Polish warning, a US spy chief's Moscow trip, and an explosive drone found beside a cargo plane at a German airport all preceded the alliance's assessment.

Kyiv • UNN
Russia attacked Kyiv and 10 regions, including with jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles. Twelve people were killed, including an Indian citizen; dozens were injured.
Russia’s nighttime attack on Ukraine using a significant number of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles claimed the lives of 12 people, including an Indian citizen, and left dozens injured, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday, reacting to another enemy strike, UNN writes.
A total of 12 people were killed, including an Indian citizen, and dozens more were injured as a result of the attack. My condolences to everyone who has lost family and loved ones
According to the President, Russia attacked Kyiv and 10 regions.
"In many cities and communities, efforts to deal with the aftermath of the Russian attack have been ongoing since the night: nearly 350 rescuers have been involved in Kyiv and the region alone. A significant number of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles were used in the strike. Unfortunately, residential and civilian infrastructure has been damaged. In Boryspil, an ordinary five-story apartment building was damaged. Fifty people were evacuated. The necessary services are on site. Businesses were also hit. In total, four people were killed and 13 injured in the city. My condolences," Zelenskyy stated, adding: "Since the evening, Odesa and the region have been subjected to strikes by guided aerial bombs and drones. Thousands of families have been left without electricity, and work is ongoing to restore it to people as quickly as possible. A border crossing with Romania was deliberately damaged, as was export infrastructure. In Kyiv, a strike on a railway depot killed seven people. The Kherson, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, Chernihiv, Zhytomyr, Sumy, and Dnipropetrovsk regions also came under fire."
Russia always calculates its strikes precisely so as to destroy lives as much as possible, and it succeeds only when air defense capabilities are insufficient. I am grateful to everyone helping Ukraine obtain antiballistic systems במסגרת PURL and bilateral deliveries, and it is very important that these supplies increase in the autumn. The number of victims of Russian terror directly depends on every new aid package. I thank everyone who helps Ukraine become more resilient

articles.title: Russia targets Ukraine’s rail network as war enters deadly new phase
articles.body:
Russia has opened a deadly new phase in its war against Ukraine by deliberately targeting the country’s railway network, with six employees killed on Tuesday in the latest strikes on Kyiv.
Ukraine’s state-owned railway company, Ukrzaliznytsia, said its workers died when a ballistic missile plunged into a locomotive depot. The Russians hit other railway facilities, it added, during a massive bombardment of Kyiv and the Kyiv region. At least 12 people died, with a dozen wounded, including three children.
“An unbearably difficult night for the entire railway family. Railway staff have been working at the scene since early this morning. The attack has caused significant damage. Rescue workers are still putting out a number of fires,” said Ukrzaliznytsia’s chair, Oleksandr Pertsovsky.
The grim strike took place as Russia escalated its attacks on the Ukrainian capital. It has carried out continuous raids for six days, beginning last week, in an attempt to disrupt daily life and demoralise the city’s inhabitants. The onslaught took place hours before Ukrainian children began a new school year.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion, 58 railway staff have been killed and at least 318 injured. One wounded railway employee, Volodymyr, was taken to hospital on Tuesday, with people urged to donate blood if they were B positive – his group. “Our colleagues are by his side,” Ukrzaliznytsia said, adding it would support victims’ families.
Ukraine’s railway network is Europe’s third largest, with 15,000 miles (24,000km) of track. It has been a lifeline for the country’s wartime civilians, transporting four million people and an estimated 120,000 pets. It has brought world leaders to Kyiv, including Joe Biden and Andy Burnham, who arrived last week on an overnight service from Poland.
Serhih Leshchenko, a member of Ukrzaliznytsia’s supervisory board, described the railway as the “backbone of Ukraine’s economy”. It was the main logistical supplier for the country’s army and industry, and every week transported 600,000 people, he told the Guardian. With 170,000 workers, it was also Ukraine’s biggest company.
For these reasons Russia was trying to destroy railways, he added. In the first year of the war it attacked bridges, which could be easily replaced. Next, it targeted rails and electricity substations. Ukraine then switched to using diesel engines. This year, Russia started “direct attacks on civilian locomotives”, he said – an insidious tactic, at a time when Ukraine is short of air defences.
Several drivers have been killed and locomotives targeted inside depots. Leshchenko said that if a Shahed drone came within 50km of a train, it had to be evacuated, and could only continue once the threat has passed. So far this year Russia has hit the network more than 1,500 times – a higher figure than in the whole of 2025. Overall, 249 carriages and 492 locomotives have been damaged.
Once known for their punctuality, trains now suffer regular delays, sometimes lasting as long as 12 to 15 hours. Amid air raid sirens, passengers are forced to disembark and take cover, including during winter. Writing on Facebook, the Ukrainian journalist Tetiana Zaiets described how she hid in April when Russian drones flew overhead.
“It was hell. The train stopped at night somewhere in central Ukraine. I don’t even know the name of the town. Half asleep, I just heard the conductor say ‘evacuation’. We took only our personal belongings and valuables with us. It was raining outside. Thank you to the conductors for handing out blankets,” she posted.
She added: “That’s how we held out for two hours. While kamikaze drones were buzzing overhead, we crawled under a goods wagon. The last carriage in the train was full of children. They were being taken back from hospital. They were crying in their sleep. I thought I’d ended up in some sort of horror film. But no, this is our life.”
Since the incident, Zaiets said she was too frightened to travel by train. “Until the war is over, I won’t be using it,” she said, stressing she respected Ukraine’s “courageous” railway workers.
Last week, an enemy drone hit a train in the Odesa region with 600 people on board, including 15 children. “The train was stopped, we were kicked out. We heard explosions, everything was burning. It was scary,” one passenger, Andriy, told the website Suspline.
Another passenger, Eva, said she was evacuated twice, and “dropped off in a field”. “We sat there and heard something flying. Then we saw a drone very close by.” She managed to collect her belongings and was eventually picked up by a bus, she said.
Leshchenko admitted the Russian strikes were hurting Ukraine’s economy and had slowed the export of grain from its under-fire Black Sea ports. He said Kyiv needed air defences from western partners, so it could protects its trains from marauding missiles and drones. “If the whole country is under attack, they will attack railways for sure,” he said.
Up until this year more than 90% of Ukrainian trains arrived on time. This was in part down to the fact engines never go especially fast, rolling at 55mph. Carriages are clean and comfortable: the best way of getting around a vast country. Stewards look after night train customers and bring them morning tea in filigree holders. There is a trolley on day trains, and patchy wifi.
On international services, border guards scrutinise male passengers, while dogs roam up and down corridors. Since the invasion, men between 18 and 60 have been forbidden from leaving the country, with some exemptions. On trains from Kyiv to Przemyśl, a railway hub in eastern Poland, most travellers are women. Since 2022 about six million people have departed abroad, many exiting by train.
In recent days Russia has launched over 1,500 drones at Ukraine, 800 of them jet-fuel models, which are harder to shoot down. In the past, Moscow would send a swarm of drones a couple of times a week, usually at night. Now the attacks continue without a pause, with one or two drones dispatched every hour, paralysing ordinary life. Air raid sirens in Kyiv are non-stop.
Pertsovsky, Ukrzaliznytsia’s boss, described the loss of his employees on Tuesday as “terrible”. “We are in touch with their loved ones. Everyone is with them to get through this extremely difficult time. The night is bitter with impossibility,” he wrote.

articles.title: CENTCOM begins wave of strikes on Iran in retaliation for targeting of US troops in region
articles.body:
US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced that it began a wave of strikes against Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in Iran on Tuesday.
According to CENTCOM, the strikes are being carried out in retaliation for Iranian attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the recent attack on US troops stationed in the region.
Iranian state media reported that several explosions were heard in the eastern area of the city of Bandar Abbas.
US President Donald Trump later confirmed the strikes in a post to Truth Social, noting that they came in retaliation for Iran's attempt to fire sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz and launch missiles at the US base in Jordan earlier this week.
"The United States is, as we speak, striking Iranian Targets near the Strait of Hormuz," he wrote. "The strikes are large and powerful, and in retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait, which currently has no mines (They have been completely removed or detonated!), and the Iranians shooting eight missiles, all successfully knocked down, at our Military Base in Jordan."
Trump threatened Iran that, should it respond to the "very justified attack," it will be hit "again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran!"
Iran will respond to the US' newest wave of strikes with an attack "several times larger," the semi-official Tasnim news outlet reported on Tuesday night, citing a senior Iranian military source.
In a statement shared by Tasnim, the General Staff of Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters stated that it would "deliver crushing and devastating blows to the despicable and malevolent American enemy."
"The more the terrorist US military persists in its malign activities in the region, the heavier the losses it will be forced to bear."
"We have repeatedly declared, and are resolved, that under no circumstances will we yield on the rights of the heroic Iranian nation, and we will impose a heavy cost on the American enemy," it stated.
US strikes Iranian launchers on Larak Island
On Sunday, the US launched its first strikes against Iran in weeks, targeting two launchers on Larak Island after IRGC forces were identified as preparing the launchers to fire towards the Strait of Hormuz.
In response, Iran launched a number of missiles towards US troops and military assets stationed in Jordan.
Trump on Monday confirmed that all but one of the missiles were intercepted by US air defense systems and that nothing of importance was hit during the attack, during a Monday phone call with Fox News’s Trey Yingst.
Trump vowed that the US would “hit [Iran] hard’ in retaliation for their attempt to target US troops.

articles.title: US launches new airstrikes on Iranian targets as hostilities flare
articles.body:
The US launched new airstrikes on Iranian targets on Tuesday, quashing hopes that an exchange of fire last weekend might not presage a wider renewal of hostilities.
Oil prices had already risen after that first exchange of direct attacks since July and after reports of two tankers being hit leaving the strait of Hormuz, the global oil supply waterway that Iran has effectively closed to shipping.
Tehran remained defiant, warning that it would prevent oil being exported from the Gulf, despite a threat by Donald Trump to hit Iran “hard” in response to the renewed Iranian strikes, and a warning from Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, that Washington was about to impose new sanctions.
“Today at 12 p.m. ET (1600 GMT), U.S. forces began striking Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in Iran,” US Central Command posted on X. “The strikes follow recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region.”
Iran’s state broadcaster said there had been reports of explosions on Iran’s Qeshm Island, on the northern side of the strait.
The state-linked news agency Nour News said there had been reports of explosions in the port city of Bandar Abbas and in Chabahar, a port on the southern coast.
The six-month conflict had shifted into an economic standoff before the weekend strikes, in which US forces attacked Iran’s Larak Island on Sunday and Iran responded by launching missiles at two US airbases in Jordan.
Although he warned of a US response to the Iranian strikes, the US president also told reporters on Monday that they did not signal a return to full-scale war, and a senior Iranian source told Reuters they were a “limited and contained confrontation”.
However, Trump made dire threats against Tehran on social media. He warned that if Iran retaliates against the US’s latest strikes, “they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran”.
The ominous last part of Trump’s message was starkly reminiscent of threats the US president has made in the past that could amount to war crimes if carried out, including threatening to destroy critical civilian infrastructure such as power plants and bridges, threatening to bomb Iran “back to the Stone Ages”, and an April threat that “a whole civilization will die tonight” if a peace deal wasn’t reached.
In Iran, the Fars news agency quoted an IRGC spokesperson as saying the US “will regret its new attacks”.
More recently pledges by both sides to respond to further attacks have highlighted how quickly a conflict that has increasingly been fought through sanctions, blockades and economic pressure could spill back into military action.
Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, had said early on Tuesday that Tehran would reciprocate immediately if Washington honoured its commitments under a June memorandum of understanding (MOU) that was intended to halt the conflict.
The MOU declared an end to fighting that has now killed thousands in Iran and Lebanon since US and Israeli strikes began on 28 February. But it also deferred many of the most difficult issues and paved the way for a broader 60-day negotiation period – which passed without further agreement.
“I am stating clearly that if the US returns to its commitments under the memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately reciprocate,” Pezeshkian said in the Kyrgyz capital, Bishkek, at a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, which includes Russia and China.
But Iranian officials have shown no public sign of bowing to pressure.
“If the enemy wants us not to export oil from the Persian Gulf, no one will be able to export oil,” Mohammad Baqer QalibafIran’s parliament speaker was quoted as saying by Iranian media. If the US intensified its “siege”, he said Tehran would respond militarily.
Esmaeil Baghaei, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, told a press conference in Tehran that Washington was “addicted to making excessive demands and has mistaken negotiations for dictating terms”.
“As long as they act in this manner, they will certainly get no result other than what they have achieved so far,” he added, warning that Tehran would “use all our capabilities, whether on the battlefield or through our diplomatic apparatus”.
Reuters contributed reporting

articles.title: Ukraine’s air defenses top EU security talks
articles.body:
EU defense ministers gathered in Ireland on Sept. 1 to discuss Ukraine’s shortage of air-defense missiles and suspected hybrid attacks across Europe as Russia stepped up its strikes on the country.
Foreign ministers are due to continue the talks on Sept. 2. The informal meetings in Wicklow are being held under Ireland’s rotating EU presidency.
Ukraine has been running low on U.S.-made interceptor missiles, limiting its ability to counter Russian attacks. Kyiv has responded with long-range strikes on Russian infrastructure.
Russian attacks were becoming “harsher and harsher,” an EU official said on condition of anonymity.
Defense ministers were expected to speak with Ukrainian Defense Minister Evgeniy Khmara. Officials said there was little immediate prospect of a large increase in interceptor deliveries beyond pressing European countries with remaining stocks and asking countries such as Japan and South Korea to contribute more.
The talks will also address what European officials describe as an increase in Russian sabotage, cyberattacks and other operations below the threshold of open conflict.
EU officials said they saw no indication that Moscow was preparing a conventional attack on the bloc in the near term but expected such operations to continue.
The issue gained attention after an explosive-laden drone was found at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany in August. Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Germany had increasingly “found itself in the crosshairs of hybrid attackers.”
Berlin has not formally blamed Russia for the incident, and the investigation remains underway.
The EU is also considering further sanctions against Moscow. Officials have floated plans to add about 1,600 Russian individuals and entities, largely linked to the country’s defense industry, to the bloc’s sanctions list.
Several member states have also revived calls to use more than 200 billion euros ($235 billion) in frozen Russian central bank assets to finance Ukraine. An earlier proposal stalled over opposition from Belgium, where most of the assets are held.
The EU instead agreed last year to provide Kyiv with a 90-billion-euro loan intended to cover two years. Some governments now argue that the bloc may need to revisit the frozen-assets proposal as the cost of supporting Ukraine rises.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha are expected to join the foreign ministers’ talks.

articles.title: America has the power to defeat Iran. Why can’t it use it?
articles.body:
America has the power to defeat Iran. Why can’t it use it?
The war against Iran, launched by the United States and Israel six months ago, was conceived as a lightning campaign against a weakened and already battered enemy.
As far as is currently known, the immediate trigger was the unrest that swept Iran in January, which appears to have convinced the Israeli and American leadership that the government in Tehran was teetering on the brink of collapse and required only a final push.
At the beginning of the campaign, Donald Trump confidently predicted that the war would last a month or six weeks, and sometimes suggested it could be over even sooner. Instead, it’s become one of the defining events of the 21st century and its long-term consequences may ultimately prove comparable to those of the September 11 attacks or Russia’s military operation in Ukraine, and perhaps even surpass them.
Among the most important consequences is the damage inflicted on the United States’ position as the principal guarantor of security for the Arab states of the Persian Gulf, a role Washington gradually assumed after the Second World War, initially alongside Britain and later largely on its own.
The war has exposed two fundamental weaknesses in that first, the United States has proved unable to protect the oil infrastructure and essential services of the Gulf monarchies from devastating attacks by a middle-ranking power such as Iran, and second, it has failed to guarantee freedom of commercial navigation in strategically important waters against attacks by Iran and its Houthi allies in Yemen.
This is important far beyond the military sphere where America’s role as the Gulf’s security guarantor, spectacularly demonstrated during Operation Desert Storm in 1990-91, became one of the foundations of the post-Cold War international order. It influenced not only the foreign policies of the Arab monarchies but their financial decisions, as they invested enormous sums in the United States partly because their relationship with Washington provided them with security.
The scale of the American commitment in 1990 illustrates how much has changed.
To defend Saudi Arabia and defeat Iraq, the United States concentrated about 540,000 troops in the region, roughly a quarter of the active-duty strength of the US armed forces at the time. Seven of the Army’s 18 active divisions and two of the Marine Corps’ three divisions participated, while six of America’s 15 aircraft carriers were deployed, along with approximately 1,600 of its 6,500 combat aircraft.
Desert Storm was ultimately an overwhelming American victory achieved at remarkably low human cost, but American planners didn’t know beforehand that casualties would be so limited. Pre-war estimates envisaged as many as 20,000 casualties, including 6,000 to 7,000 dead, but despite those projections and substantial opposition in Congress, President George H.W. Bush and his administration went ahead.
The contrast with today is amazing as the United States is no longer capable of assembling anything resembling its 1990 force in the Middle East. Around 50,000 American personnel have been deployed for the current operation against Iran, supported by approximately 300 aircraft and just over 20 warships, including two aircraft carriers.
Nor has Washington managed to mobilize its allies on anything approaching the same scale, while Britain alone contributed about 35,000 personnel to the campaign against Iraq in 1990, no American ally from outside the Middle East has made a comparable contribution to the present war.
There has therefore been a radical decline in the resources the leading Western power can mobilize to defend what it regards as vital global interests, as well as in its ability to draw upon allied military power.
Curiously, this has happened without a comparable decline in America’s share of global military expenditure, given the United States accounted for roughly 35-37% of world military spending in 1990 and around 33% in 2025. This discrepancy should encourage greater skepticism about attempts to measure military power simply by comparing defense budgets.
Yet resources are only part of the explanation as more important is Washington’s apparent inability to use effectively the formidable capabilities it still possesses.
The United States undoubtedly retains the technical capacity to inflict a crushing military defeat on Iran and overthrow its government through a sufficiently large joint military operation, even with substantially fewer forces than it deployed against Iraq in 1990, but the obstacle is the price.
Any decisive operation involving a substantial ground component would probably produce many thousands of American casualties, including hundreds, and more likely thousands, of deaths. The political system that accepted such risks in 1990 appears unwilling to accept them today.
The extraordinary effort mounted on April 5, 2026, to rescue the pilot of an F-15 shot down by Iran illustrates the problem, as the United States reportedly committed 176 aircraft to the rescue and lost three manned aircraft and two or three helicopters, representing some $300 million worth of equipment.
The determination to save individual servicemen is understandable, but a military cannot expend resources on that scale to prevent individual casualties while simultaneously fighting a major war intended to achieve decisive strategic objectives.
The same caution is visible elsewhere, seeing as American troops have been kept away from the most dangerous areas, while US warships have operated at considerable distances from the Iranian coast, reducing their effectiveness. Washington has also sought to minimize public attention to its casualties, despite their relatively small number, in marked contrast with its approach during the much more dangerous operations of the early 1990s.
Then there is the financial constraint. The 1990-91 Gulf campaign cost the US budget about $64 billion, or around $120 billion when indirect costs are included. Adjusted for inflation, that would exceed $300 billion today. By mid-July, the current operation against Iran had already cost approximately $37 billion. The total is now likely between $40 billion and $50 billion, even though the campaign has failed to produce the decisive result originally envisaged.
The lesson is therefore more complicated than the simple claim that American military power has disappeared because the United States retains enormous military and financial resources. What’s changed is its ability to concentrate those resources, mobilize allies, and accept the human and financial costs required to achieve decisive political objectives.
Desert Storm demonstrated what American military supremacy looked like at its height, but the war against Iran is revealing something very different, a superpower that can still inflict enormous damage, but increasingly struggles to convert its military superiority into the political outcomes it seeks.
This article was first published by the magazine Profile and was translated and edited by the RT team.

articles.title: Air Force spokesperson says all cruise missiles were shot down during overnight attack on Ukraine
articles.body:
Air Force spokesperson says all cruise missiles were shot down during overnight attack on Ukraine
According to Ukrinform, Yurii Ihnat, head of the Communications Department of the Ukrainian Air Force Command, said this on Ukrainian television.
"We are reporting the results of missile interceptions. There were some today. Unfortunately, not as many as we would have liked. We would like to shoot down more, but that requires more capabilities, particularly more Patriot interceptor missiles. As you can see, ballistic missiles were also intercepted today. In fact, all cruise missiles were shot down. These included Kalibr missiles, while some Banderol missiles were also hit, along with a large number of drones. The interception rate remains high, despite the fact that the enemy changed its tactics today and is using many jet-powered UAVs," Ihnat said.
He noted that many ballistic missiles failed to reach their targets.
"Today, in addition to the conventional Iskander-M ballistic missiles, the enemy is using North Korean KN-23 missiles, Zircon missiles, which attack along a ballistic trajectory and approach their targets more accurately, as well as S-400 missiles. The enemy is using a considerable number of S-400 missiles, and a large number of missiles fail to reach their targets. Therefore, information on the number of missiles launched will continue to be released selectively," Ihnat explained.
He recalled that the Ukrainian Air Force provides round-the-clock, real-time information on aerial threats.
Earlier reports said that Ukrainian air defense forces neutralized five ballistic missiles, two Banderol missiles, five Kalibr cruise missiles and 187 drones used by Russian forces to attack Ukraine from the evening of August 31.

articles.title: Why is the world rooting for Iran to win?
articles.body:
Why is the world rooting for Iran to win?
TEHRAN – Six months later, Trump finds himself trapped in a losing war with no end in sight. Officials around the world are relieved that Iran’s successful resistance has effectively prevented Trump from moving on to his next targets.
On August 26, 2026, John Mearsheimer, professor of political science at the University of Chicago, appeared as a guest on the Deep Dive geopolitics podcast hosted by retired U.S. Army Colonel Daniel Davis. The two covered the usual topics of the moment: Iran, Ukraine, and Trump’s foreign policy.
Davis, who returned from Afghanistan and, in 2012, exposed how senior U.S. military leaders had misled Congress and the American public about the course of the war there, found himself, as often happens in such discussions, trying with his guest to make sense of American’s strategically irrational policies.
Both agreed that the United States is destined to fail in both Iran and Ukraine, largely because of America’s tendency to pursue reckless and aggressive policies.
Mearsheimer also stressed that America’s global standing has sunk so low that people across the world are actively rooting for the United States and the Israeli regime to lose their war against Iran.
America’s unchecked threats
For Trita Parsi, vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft in Washington, the issue is not Iran but the threat posed to others by an America that is unconstrained, or, more accurately, unrestrained to everyone else.
Parsi said he was “stunned” by the number of officials from a wide variety of countries who have privately expressed to him a huge sigh of relief over Tehran’s success in thwarting U.S.-Israeli aggression.
Given that many of these officials represent countries that traditionally support the United States and may even have their own issues with the Islamic Republic, this “implicit endorsement” for Iran says something about the current state of international relations.
There is a sense of relief that aggression and violations of international law have failed to pay off for the U.S. and Israel in Iran.
Venezuela was, in the eyes of many, a frightening precedent. Whatever one’s opinion of Maduro, the idea of a superpower kidnapping another country’s president and his wife, installing its preferred president, who must now obtain the U.S. secretary of state’s approval for her social media posts, and then having Trump gleefully declare that Venezuela had become American territory horrified many nations.
So, too, was the praise from European leaders for the regime-change operation and their disregard for concerns about its legitimacy.
Europe, which broadly opposed George W. Bush’s illegal invasion of Iraq, has now supported regime change in Venezuela while insisting on the sanctity of international law in Ukraine and Greenland.
The lack of resistance to this made the cost of America’s new colonial-style aggression more bearable. Given Donald Trump’s inclinations, both America’s friends and foes alike feared they could be next.
A losing war with no end
America’s overwhelming military success in Venezuela was one reason Trump and the Zionist lobby were so eager for war with Iran.
If Venezuela had taken only a few hours, he figured Iran would take several days at most. Trump assured skeptical regional leaders that the entire ordeal would not last more than 100 hours, according to one anonymous Arab official.
Six months later, Trump finds himself trapped in a losing war with no end in sight. Officials around the world are relieved that Iran’s successful resistance has effectively prevented Trump from moving on to his next targets.
As one official from a traditional U.S. ally put it: “Had it not been for the resilience of the Iranians, Trump would likely have attacked Cuba by now and perhaps even annexed Greenland.”
These sympathetic feelings toward Iran may have little to do with Iran itself. No overt “official” sympathy for the Islamic Republic is visible, although the public mood seems entirely different. Rather, these sentiments are rooted in pure self-interest.
America’s pursuit of a blatant new colonial foreign policy poses a greater threat to many countries than Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz. There is no doubt that the closure harms countries that played no role in encouraging Trump’s disastrous war.
But it is relatively bearable pain. Few states besides Iran have designed their militaries to repel American or Israeli aggression should they land on Trump’s target list. Experts believe that many countries now secretly hope Trump remains bogged down in the Persian Gulf for the foreseeable future. That may be the most effective guarantee against Trump’s rush toward regime change and land grabs.
America: The most immediate threat
We are witnessing a world yearning for balance. From the perspective of many countries, not just the Global South, the United States is the country that most urgently needs to be balanced in the face of its influence and expansion. Not Russia, not Iran, and not North Korea. Certainly not China.
This is simply an objective and accurate assessment of the most immediate source of threat.
A similar situation emerged in 2022, when Russia waged a special military operation in Ukraine. Some countries sympathized with Ukraine. Others placed part of the blame on NATO. But they did not view Russia as a threat to themselves.
Then Washington severed Russia’s ties to the international financial system within five days, setting alarm bells ringing in capitals around the world. Not because they sympathized with Russia or believed the sanctions were unjustified. It was because the United States had demonstrated its ability to damage global economies within days, given the role of the dollar and Washington’s threats to the international community.
Russia’s war in Ukraine exposed no comparable vulnerability among Global South countries to Russian schemes. Yet Washington’s swift response with sanctions revealed the enormous vulnerability of other countries to U.S. whims and capabilities. Essentially, friendship with America offers no shield against Trump’s mood swings.
A Western diplomat told Parsi that she had been trying to persuade her leadership not to push for a “state visit” to Washington. “Nothing good can come of it. It’s simply better not to be on his radar,” the diplomat from a U.S.-allied country said.
As in the jungle, there is protection in avoiding the attention of the top predator. This reality once again demonstrates how disastrous the war on Iran, and neoconservative foreign policy more broadly, has been for the United States itself.
But good governance and wise diplomacy ensure that power is not unjustifiably perceived as a threat by other countries, which will have no choice but to find ways to balance it. Or, as we are seeing now, to balance it through others.
Perhaps Iran and the world do not want America to be defeated and humiliated. Perhaps they simply want it balanced, restrained, and non-aggressive.

articles.title: China сomments on Finnish President’s statement on Russia’s nuclear weapons use
articles.body:
China сomments on Finnish President’s statement on Russia’s nuclear weapons use
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said this at a media briefing in response to a question about the Finnish leader’s statement, according to Ukrinform.
“Following the meeting between Foreign Minister Wang Yi and the President of Finland [on July 5 – Ed.], we issued a press release,” Guo said in response to Ukrinform’s request to comment on Stubb’s remarks about China’s non-public position regarding Russia’s nuclear weapons.
The Chinese diplomat did not deny Stubb’s claims, merely noting that Beijing’s position on the Russia-Ukraine conflict and nuclear weapons remains unchanged.
“China’s position on the ‘Ukraine crisis’ [the official term used by China for Russia’s war against Ukraine – Ed.] and on the use of nuclear weapons is consistent and clear. We continue to call for peace talks and a political settlement of the conflict,” the foreign ministry spokesperson said.
The Chinese authorities declare adherence to a defensive nuclear doctrine and a no-first-use policy, which means that China’s nuclear arsenal would be used exclusively in retaliation for a nuclear attack against China.
The official Chinese Foreign Ministry statement on Wang Yi’s meeting with Stubb on July 5 does not mention either Russia’s war or nuclear weapons.
“The current international landscape is marked by changes and turbulence, and the world risks returning to the law of the jungle. China will continue to be an important force for peace, stability and development in today’s world,” China’s top diplomat said to the Finnish president at the time.
See also: Kuchma explains why abandoning the Budapest Memorandum would not have saved Ukraine from war
As previously reported by Ukrinform, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said that China had assured him in private talks that it would not allow Russia to use nuclear weapons.

articles.title: Von der Leyen and NATO secretary general will meet on 2 September to discuss rising hybrid threats from Russia
articles.body:
Von der Leyen and NATO secretary general will meet on 2 September to discuss rising hybrid threats from Russia
European Commission chief spokesperson Paula Pinho said that the meeting between European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte on 2 September will focus primarily on the growing hybrid threats posed by Russia to Europe and strengthening EU-NATO defence cooperation.
Source: European Pravda
Quote from Pinho: "Indeed, and it's frequently the case that meetings are added to the calendar of President von der Leyen also at short notice. Now, this meeting tomorrow between the president and Secretary General Rutte is to be seen in the context as we strengthen our defense cooperation within Europe and with NATO."
Details: The spokeswoman stressed that this is particularly important in light of the "increasing hybrid threats that we are seeing".
"So it's in this context that it's taking place. I cannot prejudge what will be discussed specifically," she added.
Asked whether Ukraine and its need for interceptor missiles would be discussed at the meeting, Paula Pinho noted that she does not "think that there can be such a discussion without referring to Ukraine, without referring to what is going on in Europe, which obviously has major consequences also for us in the EU".
Background:
- EU chief diplomat Kaja Kallas announced the creation of a high-level group made up of former political and military leaders from European countries and Ukraine, who will work on issues related to the bloc's defence capabilities.
- On 28 July, the US Department of Defense officially began a six-month review of its military presence in Europe, which could pave the way for a reduction in US troops on the continent.
- The Pentagon's review of the deployment of US troops in Europe, which is expected to be completed by 6 November, will create at least four possible courses of action for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.

articles.title: Russia Returns Nuclear-Powered Cruiser Admiral Nakhimov to Navy Service After 27 Years of Repairs
articles.body:
Russia is preparing to bring back the nuclear-powered missile cruiser Admiral Nakhimov to the Russian Navy after nearly 27 years of repairs and modernization.
Russian media outlet Novye Izvestia reported on this.
It is expected to enter service with the Russian Navy by the end of 2026, following trials.
During the modernization, the cruiser received new radar systems, an AK-192M 130 mm naval gun mount, and new missile armament.
Instead of the 20 P-700 Granit anti-ship missiles, the vessel received vertical launching systems. These allow it to deploy Kalibr, Oniks, and hypersonic Zircon missiles.
According to Russian sources, the cruiser has 176 launch cells. Of these, 80 are intended for strike missiles, while another 96 are allocated for S-400 surface-to-air missiles.
Thus, following its modernization, Admiral Nakhimov is expected to combine the capabilities of a long-range strike missile carrier and a powerful air-defense vessel.
The cruiser can also operate Ka-27 or Ka-31 helicopters. The latter are equipped with a radar system that extends the detection range for airborne and surface targets and relays information to the ship’s weapon systems.
At the same time, Admiral Nakhimov is not designed to operate entirely on its own. Given its importance and size, the cruiser will require escort ships to protect it from underwater, surface, and airborne threats.
Russia may attach particular importance to its deployment in the Arctic. After returning to service with the Russian Navy, Admiral Nakhimov could become one of the fleet’s flagship assets.
Admiral Nakhimov is the third ship of the Project 1144 Orlan. It was laid down in 1983 at the Baltic Shipyard in Leningrad, launched in 1986, and commissioned into the Soviet Navy in 1988 under the name Kalinin.
In 1992, the ship was renamed in honor of Russian Admiral Pavel Nakhimov.
Project 1144 Orlan cruisers are large nuclear-powered missile ships designed to engage major surface targets, provide air and anti-submarine defense, and perform command functions.
Admiral Nakhimov belongs to Russia’s Northern Fleet, but has spent most of its service life undergoing repairs. Modernization work began back in 1999, with the active phase starting only in 2013 at the Sevmash facility in Severodvinsk.
The modernization was initially scheduled for completion in 2018, but the deadline was repeatedly postponed — first to 2020, then to 2021, 2022, 2024, and 2025. As of 2025, the total cost of the work had exceeded RUB 200 billion.
In 2024–2025, Admiral Nakhimov went to sea for trials after undergoing extensive repairs.
